## 13. Discussion

### 13.1 A pattern: overlapping disjunctions

Three of the central results share a shape. Cotransitivity (Theorem 6.5) concludes "$x < z$ **or** $z < y$", and both may hold. Constructive location concludes "$a < x$ **or** $x < b$" for $a < b$, and both may hold. The located datum (Definition 10.1) concludes "$q$ is an upper bound **or** some member exceeds $p$", and both may hold.

In each case the classical statement is an exclusive dichotomy that is undecidable, and the constructive replacement is an *overlapping* disjunction that is decidable. The overlap is not a defect; it is the mechanism. A decision procedure needs slack in order to be implementable, and the size of the slack is the quantitative content: $\frac{g}{8}$ in cotransitivity, $\frac{b-a}{4}$ in location, $q - p$ in locatedness. Theorem 11.4 says something remarkable about this: the slack in the located datum forces a strictly positive information loss, but the loss can be made arbitrarily small.

### 13.2 Where the classical proofs hide their hypotheses

Each constructive theorem here has a classical counterpart with strictly fewer hypotheses, and in each case the missing hypothesis is one the classical proof consumes invisibly:

- **Completeness.** Classically, no modulus is required; constructively, the modulus is the datum and the diagonal shift is forced (Theorem 4.4).
- **Intermediate value theorem.** Classically, continuity suffices; constructively, one needs a modulus *and* either to weaken the conclusion to $\varepsilon$-approximation (Theorem 7.2) or to add a slope bound (Theorem 7.6). The shelf family (Theorem 8.4) shows this is not an artefact of proof technique.
- **Least upper bound.** Classically, boundedness suffices; constructively, locatedness is needed, and Theorem 10.9 shows that classically it is free.

The uniform diagnosis: the classical proof performs an undecidable decision, and the constructive theorem either supplies that decision as data or weakens the conclusion until the decision is unnecessary.

### 13.3 Sharpness as a dividend

The results of Sections 4.4, 7.3, 9 and 11 are of a kind that cannot even be *stated* in a purely existential development. "The constant $\varepsilon/c$ is attained" presupposes that a constant has been named. "The shift $2n+1$ cannot be removed" presupposes that the limit is given by a formula. "$2/3$ is not optimal" presupposes an algorithm with a rate. Making the constructions explicit does not merely make them implementable; it makes them *criticisable*, and the criticism yields new mathematics.

### 13.4 Limitations

Our metatheory is classical: we prove classical statements about constructive data, and we use the classical intermediate value theorem to produce the exact root whose *location* is then computed constructively (Theorem 7.6, Theorem 9.1). A fully intuitionistic treatment would construct the root by the search itself. This is a difference of packaging rather than of content — the algorithms and their bounds are unchanged, and the sharpness statements (which quantify over all functions or all constants) are most naturally classical anyway.

## 14. Future directions

The following are concrete, falsifiable conjectures suggested by the development. Each is stated so that a single proof or a single counterexample settles it.

### C6. $k$ oracle calls per step cannot beat the ratio $1/(k+1)$

Theorem 11.4 shows that the optimal contraction ratio of a *one-query* located search is the infimum $1/2$, never attained. The natural generalisation queries the locatedness oracle $k$ times per step, at the pairs $\bigl(p + \alpha_i (q-p),\, p + \beta_i (q-p)\bigr)$ with $\alpha_1 < \beta_1 \le \alpha_2 < \beta_2 \le \cdots < \beta_k$, keeping the smallest enclosure the answers certify.

> **Conjecture.** The worst-case contraction factor of any such $k$-query scheme is $> \frac{1}{k+1}$, and for every $\eta > 0$ some $k$-query scheme achieves a factor $< \frac{1}{k+1} + \eta$. In particular the per-oracle-call efficiency $(\text{contraction})^{1/k}$ tends to $0$ as $k \to \infty$: batching queries strictly pays.

Falsifiable: a $k$-query scheme (for a concrete $k$, e.g. $k = 2$) that provably preserves the enclosure invariant and contracts by a factor $\le \frac{1}{k+1}$ refutes the first half; a proof that no $2$-query scheme beats, say, $2/5$ refutes the second.

### C7. The cotransitivity threshold is exactly $6$

Theorem 6.5 decides $x < z$ or $z < y$ at any index $m$ with $\frac{1}{m+1} \le \frac{g}{8}$, where $g$ is the certified gap; the arithmetic of the proof only needs $\frac{1}{m+1} < \frac{g}{6}$.

> **Conjecture.** $6$ is optimal: the hypothesis $\frac{1}{m+1} \le \frac{g}{\kappa}$ with $\kappa < 6$ is insufficient — there are $x, y, z$ and indices $n, m$ satisfying it for which the midpoint test at $m$ decides neither $x < z$ nor $z < y$ — while the conclusion of cotransitivity does hold under $\frac{1}{m+1} < \frac{g}{6}$.

Falsifiable: a proof of cotransitivity with a constant $\kappa < 6$ refutes the first half; an explicit triple defeating the constant $6$ refutes the second.

### C8. The canonical multiplication bound can be lowered to $\lceil |x_0| \rceil + 1$

The bound $B(x) = \lceil |x_0| \rceil + 2$ of Definition 3.4 is used to choose the index shift in the definition of multiplication. Since $|x_n - x_0| \le \frac{1}{n+1} + 1 \le 2$, with strict inequality for $n \ge 1$, only $n = 0$ is at issue.

> **Conjecture.** Replacing $B$ by $\lceil |x_0| \rceil + 1$ still yields a regular sequence for the product, and the identification of the product with $\hat x \hat y$ continues to hold; the constant $1$ is then optimal, i.e. $\lceil |x_0| \rceil$ alone fails for some pair of Bishop reals.

Falsifiable: a pair $x, y$ for which the sequence defined with $\lceil |x_0| \rceil + 1$ violates the regularity inequality refutes the first half; a proof that $\lceil |x_0| \rceil$ always suffices refutes the second.

### Further questions

- **Sharpness of the addition shift.** Is $n \mapsto 2n+1$ the least shift for which the pointwise sum of two regular sequences is regular? The analogue of Theorem 4.4 for addition is open.
- **Uniformity in the shelf oscillation.** Theorem 8.5 gives oscillation $\ge 1$ for every root selector. Is $1$ the exact value of the oscillation infimum over all selectors, and is it attained by the discontinuous selector of Section 8.3?
- **Bracket-based moduli.** Theorem 9.1 gives location to within one mesh with no non-degeneracy hypothesis. Can the whole of Theorem 7.6 be rederived from bracketing alone, with the slope bound entering only in the uniqueness statement?

---

## 15. Conclusion

We have carried out a quantitative development of Bishop's constructive analysis in which every existence statement is accompanied by an explicit modulus: real numbers as regular sequences with the canonical rate $1/(n+1)$; completeness by the shifted diagonal $n \mapsto x^{(2n+1)}_{2n+1}$, with the shift shown necessary; an order carrying certificates, with an explicit cotransitivity algorithm and a proof that the certificate cannot be bounded in advance; the intermediate value theorem in its approximate form (always available, by finite grid search) and its exact form (available under a slope bound, with root modulus $\delta \mapsto \omega(c\delta)$ and the sharp displacement bound $\varepsilon/c$); a Brouwerian counterexample whose failure is quantified to oscillation $\ge 1$; a bracketing refinement showing that sign changes locate roots better than residuals do, with an explicit function proving local non-constancy insufficient; and the least upper bound principle for located sets, with the exact rate $(2/3)^n$ improved to $\max(\beta, 1-\alpha)^n$ and the optimal ratio identified as the unattained infimum $1/2$.

The recurring theme is that explicitness is not merely a philosophical constraint but a mathematical instrument. Once a rate is written down, one can ask whether it is optimal; once an algorithm is written down, one can ask whether it is efficient. The classical theorems, which assert only that something exists, do not admit these questions. Bishop's discipline turns analysis into a subject with constants — and constants can be improved.

\begin{abstract}
We present a self-contained quantitative development of Errett Bishop's constructive real analysis, organised around the principle that every existence claim must be accompanied by an explicit modulus. Real numbers are taken to be \emph{regular sequences of rationals}, sequences $x:\N\to\Q$ satisfying $|x_m-x_n|\le\frac1{m+1}+\frac1{n+1}$, so that the modulus of Cauchyness is part of the datum rather than an object produced by a non-effective search. We establish: the explicit approximation bound $|\hat x-x_n|\le\frac1{n+1}$; the equivalence of Bishop equality $|x_n-y_n|\le\frac2{n+1}$ with equality of denoted reals, whence the quotient of regular sequences by Bishop equality is in canonical bijection with $\R$; constructive completeness by the shifted diagonal $n\mapsto x^{(2n+1)}_{2n+1}$ with the estimate $|L-\hat x^{(k)}|\le\frac1{k+1}$, together with an explicit family showing the shift cannot be removed; the witnessed order, its extensional agreement with the classical order, an explicit cotransitivity algorithm requiring one rational comparison at any index $m$ with $\frac1{m+1}\le\frac g8$, and the impossibility of any uniform bound on the witness index; the approximate intermediate value theorem by an explicit finite grid search, and the exact intermediate value theorem under a positive slope bound $c$, with root modulus $\delta\mapsto\omega(c\delta)$ and the sharp displacement estimate $|x-r|\le\varepsilon/c$; a Brouwerian counterexample showing that no continuous, hence no constructive, root selector exists, strengthened to the statement that \emph{every} root selector has oscillation at least $1$ in every neighbourhood of the critical parameter; a bracketing refinement showing that the sign-change grid search locates a genuine root to within one mesh \emph{without any non-degeneracy hypothesis}, and an explicit function proving that local non-constancy is by itself insufficient for any ``small value implies near a root'' principle; and the constructive least upper bound principle for located sets via a trisection search with exact geometric rate $(2/3)^n$, together with a complete analysis of the general one-query search: the contraction factor with query fractions $\alpha<\beta$ is exactly $\max(\beta,1-\alpha)$, trisection is not optimal, and the optimal contraction factor of a one-query located search is the infimum $\tfrac12$, never attained.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} constructive analysis; Bishop reals; regular sequences; explicit modulus; intermediate value theorem; Brouwerian counterexample; located sets; cotransitivity; computable reals.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The problem of effective content}

Classical analysis proves existence statements. It proves that a Cauchy sequence converges, that a continuous function changing sign has a root, that a bounded set has a supremum. What it typically does not do is say \emph{how} --- at what rate, from what index, with what precision.

The gap is easy to locate. The classical definition of a Cauchy sequence reads
\[
\forall \varepsilon>0\ \exists N\ \forall m,n\ge N:\ |x_m-x_n|<\varepsilon,
\]
and the object $N$ --- the \emph{modulus of convergence} --- is bound by an unrestricted existential quantifier. A classical proof may produce that $N$ by any means, including an appeal to excluded middle over an undecidable predicate. There is then no function $\varepsilon\mapsto N(\varepsilon)$ available, and no way to compute the limit to a prescribed accuracy.

Bishop's response, developed in \emph{Foundations of Constructive Analysis} (1967) and its revision with Bridges (1985), was to relocate the modulus from the conclusion into the datum. This paper carries that programme out for the core of elementary real analysis, and pushes it one step further: once every constant is explicit, one can ask whether the constants are \emph{optimal}.

\subsection{Contributions}

Much of the content below is Bishop's, restated with full quantitative detail. The following are, to our knowledge, either new or not standard:

\begin{enumerate}\renewcommand{\labelenumi}{(\arabic{enumi})}
\item \textbf{Necessity of the diagonal shift.} An explicit family of regular sequences of reals for which the unshifted diagonal $n\mapsto x^{(n)}_n$ fails regularity, at $m=0$, $n=1$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:shiftnec}).
\item \textbf{Sharpness of the root modulus.} The bound $|x-r|\le\varepsilon/c$ is attained, and no constant $\kappa<1$ replaces the implicit $1$ (Theorems~\ref{thm:attained}, \ref{thm:nosmaller}).
\item \textbf{Quantitative failure of the exact intermediate value theorem.} Every root selector, continuous or not, has oscillation at least $1$ on every neighbourhood of the critical parameter (Theorem~\ref{thm:osc}).
\item \textbf{Bracketing beats bounding.} The sign-change grid search locates a genuine root to within one mesh with no non-degeneracy hypothesis (Theorem~\ref{thm:bracket}); local non-constancy supports no ``small value implies near a root'' principle (Theorem~\ref{thm:lnc}).
\item \textbf{Optimal one-query contraction ratio.} Exactly $\max(\beta,1-\alpha)$; trisection's $2/3$ is not optimal; the infimum is $\tfrac12$ and it is not attained (Theorems~\ref{thm:gencontract}--\ref{thm:half}).
\item \textbf{No uniform witness bound for the order} (Theorem~\ref{thm:nowitness}).
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Conventions}

We work in a classical metatheory: our theorems are classical statements \emph{about} constructive data, and the comparison with classical analysis is made explicit rather than tacit. This is the natural setting for sharpness claims, which quantify over all functions or all constants. We write $\hat x$ for the classical real denoted by a regular sequence $x$.

\section{Regular sequences of rationals}

\begin{definition}[regular sequence]\label{def:reg}
A \textbf{regular sequence of rationals}, or \textbf{Bishop real}, is a sequence $x:\N\to\Q$ with
\[
|x_m-x_n| \;\le\; \frac{1}{m+1}+\frac{1}{n+1}\qquad\text{for all }m,n\in\N.
\]
\end{definition}

The intended reading: $x_n$ is an approximation, accurate to within $1/(n+1)$, of the number the sequence denotes; the inequality expresses that these accuracy claims are mutually consistent. The modulus is \emph{fixed by the definition}, not obtained by a search. If $n\mapsto x_n$ is computable, the real number is a computable object in the most concrete sense.

\begin{lemma}
The real sequence $n\mapsto x_n$ is Cauchy, with $|x_n-x_m|\le\frac{2}{N+1}$ whenever $n,m\ge N$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}
$\hat x:=\lim_n x_n\in\R$, the classical real \textbf{denoted} by $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[explicit modulus]\label{thm:modulus}
For every regular sequence $x$ and every $n$,
\[
|\hat x - x_n| \;\le\; \frac{1}{n+1}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Fix $n$ and let $j\to\infty$ in $|x_j-x_n|\le\frac1{j+1}+\frac1{n+1}$. The left side tends to $|\hat x-x_n|$ and the right to $\frac1{n+1}$; weak inequalities pass to the limit.
\end{proof}

To compute $\hat x$ to accuracy $\varepsilon$ it suffices to evaluate $x_n$ for any $n\ge\lceil 1/\varepsilon\rceil$: no search, no waiting phase.

\begin{theorem}[identification criterion]\label{thm:ident}
If $x$ is regular, $r\in\R$, $C\ge0$ and $|x_n-r|\le\frac{C}{n+1}$ for all $n$, then $\hat x=r$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:modulus} and the triangle inequality $|\hat x-r|\le\frac{1+C}{n+1}$ for all $n$; let $n\to\infty$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Bishop equality]
$x\approx y$ iff $|x_n-y_n|\le\dfrac{2}{n+1}$ for all $n$.
\end{definition}

Constructively one cannot define $x=y$ as $\hat x=\hat y$: the limits are not antecedently available, only the sequences are. The tolerance $2/(n+1)$ is the sum of the two error bars, hence forced.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:eqiff}
$x\approx y$ if and only if $\hat x=\hat y$. Consequently $\approx$ is an equivalence relation.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
($\Rightarrow$) $|\hat x-\hat y|\le|\hat x-x_n|+|x_n-y_n|+|y_n-\hat y|\le\frac{4}{n+1}$ for all $n$. ($\Leftarrow$) $|x_n-y_n|\le|x_n-\hat x|+|\hat y-y_n|\le\frac{2}{n+1}$.
\end{proof}

Transitivity is the classical ``$3\varepsilon$'' argument; here it is packaged by Theorem~\ref{thm:eqiff}. Write $\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm B}$ for the quotient.

\begin{theorem}[surjectivity]\label{thm:surj}
Every $r\in\R$ is denoted by some regular sequence.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Choose $q_n\in\Q$ with $|r-q_n|<\frac{1}{2(n+1)}$. Then $|q_m-q_n|<\frac{1}{2(m+1)}+\frac{1}{2(n+1)}\le\frac1{m+1}+\frac1{n+1}$, so $q$ is regular; Theorem~\ref{thm:ident} with $C=1$ identifies its limit.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[comparison with classical analysis]
The map $[x]\mapsto\hat x$ is a bijection $\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm B}\to\R$.
\end{theorem}

Constructive analysis is thus not a theory of \emph{fewer} numbers: it is the same numbers, presented with more information.

\section{Computable arithmetic}

\begin{definition}
For $q\in\Q$ the constant sequence $(q)_n=q$ is regular and denotes $q$; $(-x)_n=-x_n$ is regular and denotes $-\hat x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[addition]
$(x+y)_n := x_{2n+1}+y_{2n+1}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}
$x+y$ is regular and denotes $\hat x+\hat y$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$|(x+y)_m-(x+y)_n|\le 2\bigl(\tfrac1{2(m+1)}+\tfrac1{2(n+1)}\bigr)=\tfrac1{m+1}+\tfrac1{n+1}$, using $(2k+1)+1=2(k+1)$.
\end{proof}

The shift $n\mapsto 2n+1$ is exactly the halving of the error budget needed for two summands.

\begin{definition}[canonical bound]\label{def:bound}
$B(x):=\lceil |x_0| \rceil + 2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}
$|x_n|\le B(x)$ for all $n$, since $|x_n|\le|x_0|+\frac{1}{n+1}+1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[multiplication]
With $M:=B(x)+B(y)$ and $\mu(n):=M(n+1)$, set $(x\cdot y)_n := x_{\mu(n)}\,y_{\mu(n)}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}
$x\cdot y$ is regular and denotes $\hat x\,\hat y$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Write $ab-a'b'=a(b-b')+b'(a-a')$; bound $|a|,|b'|$ by $B(x),B(y)$ and each difference by regularity. The resulting bound is $M\bigl(\frac{1}{\mu(m)+1}+\frac{1}{\mu(n)+1}\bigr)$, and $M\cdot\frac{1}{M(n+1)+1}\le\frac1{n+1}$ closes the estimate.
\end{proof}

The shift is proportional to the magnitudes: larger numbers need more precision before their product is trustworthy.

\begin{example}[a computable irrational]
Let
\[
\sqrt2_n:=\frac{\bigl\lfloor \sqrt{2(n+1)^2}\bigr\rfloor}{n+1}\in\Q,
\]
the numerator being the integer square root. Then $\sqrt2$ is regular, its denoted real squares to $2$, and its terms are literally computable: $\sqrt2_4=7/5$, $\sqrt2_{99}=141/100$.
\end{example}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
With $s=\lfloor\sqrt{2m^2}\rfloor$ one has $s\le\sqrt{2m^2}<s+1$, hence $|s/m-\sqrt2|\le1/m$; take $m=n+1$ and apply Theorem~\ref{thm:ident}.
\end{proof}

\section{Constructive completeness}

\begin{definition}
A sequence $x^{(0)},x^{(1)},\dots$ of Bishop reals is a \textbf{regular sequence of reals} if $\bigl|\hat x^{(k)}-\hat x^{(l)}\bigr|\le\frac1{k+1}+\frac1{l+1}$ for all $k,l$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[constructive completeness]\label{thm:complete}
Let $x^{(\bullet)}$ be a regular sequence of reals. Then $L_n := x^{(2n+1)}_{\,2n+1}$ defines a regular sequence of rationals, and its denoted real $\hat L$ satisfies
\[
\bigl|\hat L-\hat x^{(k)}\bigr| \;\le\; \frac{1}{k+1}\qquad\text{for every }k.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:modulus}, $|x^{(2j+1)}_{2j+1}-\hat x^{(2j+1)}|\le\frac{1}{2j+2}=\frac12\cdot\frac1{j+1}$. Hence
\[
|L_m-L_n|\le \tfrac12\tfrac1{m+1}+\Bigl(\tfrac12\tfrac1{m+1}+\tfrac12\tfrac1{n+1}\Bigr)+\tfrac12\tfrac1{n+1}=\tfrac1{m+1}+\tfrac1{n+1}.
\]
For the rate, $|\hat L-\hat x^{(k)}|\le\frac1{n+1}+\frac1{2(n+1)}+\frac1{2(n+1)}+\frac1{k+1}$ for every $n$; let $n\to\infty$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[witness family]
$w^{(k)}_n := \dfrac{1}{k+1}+(-1)^k\cdot\dfrac{1}{n+1}$.
\end{definition}

Each $w^{(k)}$ is regular with $\hat w^{(k)}=\frac1{k+1}$, and the family is a regular sequence of reals.

\begin{theorem}[the diagonal shift is necessary]\label{thm:shiftnec}
For the family $w^{(\bullet)}$, the unshifted diagonal $n\mapsto w^{(n)}_n$ is \emph{not} a regular sequence: $w^{(0)}_0=2$ and $w^{(1)}_1=0$ differ by $2$, while regularity permits at most $\frac11+\frac12=\frac32$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}
For the same family the shifted diagonal converges to the correct limit, $\hat L=0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:complete}, $|\hat L-\frac{1}{k+1}|\le\frac1{k+1}$, hence $|\hat L|\le\frac2{k+1}\to0$.
\end{proof}

A constructive completeness theorem is a \emph{formula}, and the formula must budget two independent sources of error against a single allowance $1/(n+1)$. The factor $2$ is exactly the cost of two sources.

\section{Continuity with an explicit modulus}

\begin{definition}
$\omega:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ is a \textbf{modulus of uniform continuity} for $f$ on $S$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ we have $\omega(\varepsilon)>0$ and
\[
x,y\in S,\ |x-y|\le\omega(\varepsilon)\ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x)-f(y)|\le\varepsilon.
\]
\end{definition}

This is Bishop's definition of continuity on a compact interval: not the assertion that a tolerance exists, but a function producing it. A function with a modulus is continuous. Every $1$-Lipschitz function has the modulus $\omega=\mathrm{id}$; $x\mapsto cx$ ($c>0$) has $\omega(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon/c$.

\section{The constructive order}

\begin{definition}
For regular sequences,
\[
x>0 :\iff \exists n:\ x_n>\frac1{n+1};\qquad x<y :\iff \exists n:\ x_n+\frac2{n+1}<y_n.
\]
\end{definition}

A proof of $x<y$ is a pair (index, rational inequality) --- a certificate checkable by a finite computation.

\begin{theorem}[extensional agreement]\label{thm:extord}
$x>0\iff\hat x>0$, and $x<y\iff\hat x<\hat y$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
($\Rightarrow$) $\hat x\ge x_n-\frac1{n+1}>0$. ($\Leftarrow$) Pick $n$ with $\frac2{n+1}<\hat x$; then $x_n\ge\hat x-\frac1{n+1}>\frac1{n+1}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[certified gap]
If $n$ witnesses $x<y$, set $g:=y_n-x_n-\frac2{n+1}\in\Q_{>0}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[gap propagation]\label{lem:gap}
If $\frac1{m+1}\le\frac g8$ then $y_m-x_m\ge\frac{3g}{4}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\hat y-\hat x\ge g$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:modulus}; also $x_m\le\hat x+\frac1{m+1}$ and $y_m\ge\hat y-\frac1{m+1}$, so $y_m-x_m\ge g-\frac2{m+1}\ge g-\frac g4$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[cotransitivity, explicit form]\label{thm:cotrans}
Let $n$ witness $x<y$ with certified gap $g$, and let $m$ satisfy $\frac1{m+1}\le\frac g8$. Then for every regular sequence $z$ the single decidable rational comparison
\[
z_m \;\ge\; \frac{x_m+y_m}{2}\ ?
\]
decides between the certificates $x_m+\frac2{m+1}<z_m$ and $z_m+\frac2{m+1}<y_m$, so that $x<z$ or $z<y$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:gap}, $y_m-x_m\ge\frac{3g}4$, and $\frac2{m+1}\le\frac g4$. If $z_m\ge\frac{x_m+y_m}{2}$ then $z_m-x_m\ge\frac{3g}{8}>\frac g4\ge\frac2{m+1}$; symmetrically otherwise.
\end{proof}

The disjunction is \emph{overlapping} --- both branches may hold --- and that is precisely why the test is decidable. The same technique gives \textbf{constructive location}: for rationals $a<b$ and any $x$, choose $n$ with $\frac4{n+1}\le b-a$ and compare $x_n$ with $\frac{a+b}2$ to obtain $a<\hat x$ or $\hat x<b$.

\begin{theorem}[no uniform witness bound]\label{thm:nowitness}
For every $N\in\N$ there are Bishop reals $x<y$ such that no index $n\le N$ witnesses the inequality.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take $x\equiv0$ and $y\equiv\frac1{N+1}$. Then $\hat x<\hat y$, so $x<y$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:extord}. For $n\le N$, $\frac1{N+1}\le\frac1{n+1}\le\frac2{n+1}$, so $x_n+\frac2{n+1}\ge y_n$.
\end{proof}

The order, though extensionally classical, is not decidable at any bounded precision.

\section{The intermediate value theorem}

\begin{definition}
For $a\le b$, $N\ge1$: grid points $\gr_k:=a+k\frac{b-a}{N}$, $0\le k\le N$; mesh $\frac{b-a}{N}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[approximate intermediate value theorem]\label{thm:aivt}
Let $f$ have modulus $\omega$ on $[a,b]$ with $f(a)\le0\le f(b)$. Let $\varepsilon>0$ and $N\ge1$ with $\frac{b-a}{N}\le\omega(\varepsilon)$. Then the \emph{largest} index $k\le N$ with $f(\gr_k)\le0$ satisfies $|f(\gr_k)|\le\varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$S=\{k\le N: f(\gr_k)\le0\}$ contains $0$ and is finite, so has a maximum $k$. If $k=N$ then $f(b)=0$. Otherwise $f(\gr_{k+1})>0$ by maximality; the two points are one mesh apart, hence within $\omega(\varepsilon)$, so $f(\gr_{k+1})-f(\gr_k)\le\varepsilon$, and $|f(\gr_k)|=-f(\gr_k)\le\varepsilon$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[slope bound]
$f$ has \textbf{slope bound} $c$ on $S$ if $x\le y$ in $S$ implies $c(y-x)\le f(y)-f(x)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[root modulus]\label{thm:rootmod}
Let $f$ have slope bound $c>0$ on $[a,b]$, $f(r)=0$ with $r\in[a,b]$, and $|f(x)|\le\varepsilon$ with $x\in[a,b]$. Then $|x-r|\le\varepsilon/c$. In particular the root is unique.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
If $r\le x$: $c(x-r)\le f(x)-f(r)=f(x)\le\varepsilon$. If $x\le r$: $c(r-x)\le -f(x)\le\varepsilon$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[constructive intermediate value theorem with explicit modulus]\label{thm:civt}
Let $f$ have modulus $\omega$ and slope bound $c>0$ on $[a,b]$, with $f(a)\le0\le f(b)$. Then $f$ has a unique root $r\in[a,b]$, and for every $\delta>0$ and every $N\ge1$ with $\frac{b-a}{N}\le\omega(c\delta)$ the grid search at accuracy $c\delta$ returns $k\le N$ with $|\gr_k-r|\le\delta$. The modulus of the root is $\delta\mapsto\omega(c\delta)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Existence follows from continuity and the classical intermediate value theorem; uniqueness from Theorem~\ref{thm:rootmod}. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:aivt} with $\varepsilon=c\delta$, then Theorem~\ref{thm:rootmod}: $|\gr_k-r|\le c\delta/c=\delta$.
\end{proof}

Running this over $\delta=\frac{1}{2(n+1)}$ presents the root itself as a Bishop real, each of whose terms is an explicitly computed rational grid point.

\begin{theorem}[the root modulus is attained]\label{thm:attained}
For every $c>0$ and $\varepsilon>0$ with $\varepsilon/c\le1$ there is a function on $[-1,1]$ with an explicit modulus and slope bound $c$, a root $r$, and a point $x$ with $|f(x)|\le\varepsilon$ and $|x-r|=\varepsilon/c$ exactly.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$f(x)=cx$, $\omega(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon/c$, $r=0$, $x=\varepsilon/c$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[no smaller constant]\label{thm:nosmaller}
There is no $\kappa<1$ such that a slope bound $c>0$, a root $r$, and $|f(x)|\le\varepsilon$ always imply $|x-r|\le\kappa\,\varepsilon/c$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take $f(x)=x$ on $[-1,1]$, $c=\varepsilon=1$, $r=0$, $x=1$: the hypothesis gives $1\le\kappa$.
\end{proof}

\section{The Brouwerian counterexample}

\begin{definition}[shelf family]
For $t\in[-1,1]$ define $\shelf_t:[0,3]\to\R$ by
\[
\shelf_t(x)=\min\bigl(x-1,\ \max(t,\ x-2)\bigr).
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}
Each $\shelf_t$ is $1$-Lipschitz (hence has the explicit modulus $\omega=\mathrm{id}$) and satisfies $\shelf_t(0)\le0\le\shelf_t(3)$. Consequently Theorem~\ref{thm:aivt} applies \emph{uniformly in $t$}: for every $\varepsilon>0$ and every $N$ with $3/N\le\varepsilon$ some grid point of $[0,3]$ satisfies $|\shelf_t|\le\varepsilon$, and $N$ does not depend on $t$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{lemma}[root structure]\label{lem:shelfroots}
\begin{enumerate}\renewcommand{\labelenumi}{(\roman{enumi})}
\item If $t>0$ the unique root of $\shelf_t$ is $x=1$; if $t<0$ it is $x=2$.
\item If $1<x<2$ and $\shelf_t(x)=0$ then $t=0$.
\item Every root of every $\shelf_t$ lies in $[1,2]$.
\item $\shelf_0$ vanishes identically on $[1,2]$; consequently it admits \emph{no} positive slope bound on $[0,3]$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Brouwerian counterexample]\label{thm:brouwer}
There is no continuous $r:[-1,1]\to\R$ with $\shelf_t(r(t))=0$ for all $t\in[-1,1]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose such an $r$ exists. By Lemma~\ref{lem:shelfroots}, $r(1)=1$ and $r(-1)=2$. By the classical intermediate value theorem applied to $r$, the interval $[1,2]$ lies in the image; pick $t_0,t_1$ with $r(t_0)=3/2$ and $r(t_1)=7/4$. Both values lie strictly between $1$ and $2$, so $t_0=t_1=0$, whence $3/2=r(0)=7/4$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

Since every constructively definable function $\R\to\R$ is continuous, no constructive proof of the exact intermediate value theorem can exist. What rescues Theorem~\ref{thm:civt} is exactly the hypothesis this family violates.

\begin{theorem}[quantitative failure]\label{thm:osc}
Let $r:[-1,1]\to\R$ be \emph{any} function with $\shelf_t(r(t))=0$ for all $t$. Then for every $\eta>0$,
\[
\sup r\bigl([-1,1]\cap[-\eta,\eta]\bigr)-\inf r\bigl([-1,1]\cap[-\eta,\eta]\bigr)\;\ge\;1.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Set $s=\min(\eta,1)>0$; both $s$ and $-s$ lie in the parameter window, and $r(s)=1$, $r(-s)=2$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:shelfroots}. All values lie in $[1,2]$, so the supremum is $\ge2$ and the infimum $\le1$.
\end{proof}

The hypothesis is not vacuous: the discontinuous selector $r(t)=2$ for $t<0$ and $r(t)=1$ otherwise satisfies it.

\section{Bracketing versus bounding}

\begin{theorem}[bracketing form of the grid search]\label{thm:bracket}
Let $f$ have a modulus of uniform continuity on $[a,b]$ with $f(a)\le0\le f(b)$, and let $N\ge1$. Then the largest grid index $k$ with $f(\gr_k)\le0$ satisfies: there is a genuine root $r\in[a,b]$ of $f$ with
\[
|\gr_k-r|\le\frac{b-a}{N}.
\]
No non-degeneracy hypothesis is required.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
If $k=N$ then $f(b)=0$ and $r=b=\gr_k$. Otherwise $f(\gr_k)\le0<f(\gr_{k+1})$, and continuity supplies a root in $[\gr_k,\gr_{k+1}]$, an interval of length one mesh.
\end{proof}

The accuracy of the \emph{location} is the mesh itself, with no $1/c$ factor. The information used is the \emph{sign change}, not the smallness of $|f|$ --- and the difference is real.

\begin{definition}[local non-constancy]
$f$ satisfies \textbf{local non-constancy with modulus $\nu$} if $\nu(h)>0$ for $h>0$ and, for every $h>0$ and every interval $[p,q]$ with $q-p\ge h$, there is $z\in[p,q]$ with $|f(z)|\ge\nu(h)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[local non-constancy is insufficient]\label{thm:lnc}
For every $\delta\in(0,2)$ there is a $1$-Lipschitz $f$ on $[0,4]$ with $f(0)\le0\le f(4)$, satisfying local non-constancy with the explicit modulus $\nu(h)=h/8$, and a point $x\in[0,4]$ with
\[
|f(x)|\le\frac{\nu(\delta)}{2}\qquad\text{yet}\qquad |x-r|>\delta\ \text{ for every root } r.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Take $\eta:=\delta/32$ and $f=\dip_\eta$ with $\dip_\eta(x)=\min\bigl(x-1,\ |x-3|+\eta\bigr)$ on $[0,4]$. It is $1$-Lipschitz; $f(0)=-1\le0$ and $f(4)=\min(3,1+\eta)>0$; its unique root is $x=1$, since the second branch is bounded below by $\eta>0$. Local non-constancy with $\nu(h)=h/8$ holds because on any interval of length $\ge h$ one finds a point at distance $\ge h/8$ from both critical points $1$ and $3$, where $|f|\ge h/8$. Finally $f(3)=\eta=\delta/32\le\nu(\delta)/2=\delta/16$, while $|3-1|=2>\delta$.
\end{proof}

For algorithm design: report the bracket, not the residual.

\section{The constructive least upper bound principle}

\begin{definition}[located data]
A \textbf{located datum} for $S\subseteq\R$ is $L:\Q\times\Q\to\{\texttt{true},\texttt{false}\}$ such that for rationals $p<q$:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item $L(p,q)=\texttt{true}$ implies $s\le q$ for all $s\in S$;
\item $L(p,q)=\texttt{false}$ implies there is $s\in S$ with $s>p$.
\end{itemize}
\end{definition}

The two conclusions are compatible --- when $\sup S\in(p,q)$ both hold --- and that slack is what makes $L$ implementable.

\begin{definition}
$(p,q)\in\Q^2$ \textbf{encloses} $S$ if $q$ is an upper bound of $S$ and some $s\in S$ satisfies $s>p$.
\end{definition}

\begin{algorithmx}[trisection step]
Given $p<q$, set $m_1=p+\frac{q-p}{3}$, $m_2=p+\frac{2(q-p)}{3}$, and return
\[
T(p,q)=\begin{cases}(p,\,m_2)&\text{if }L(m_1,m_2)=\texttt{true},\\ (m_1,\,q)&\text{if }L(m_1,m_2)=\texttt{false}.\end{cases}
\]
Let $(p_n,q_n):=T^n(a_0,b_0)$.
\end{algorithmx}

\begin{theorem}[exact geometric rate]\label{thm:rate}
$q_n-p_n=\left(\frac23\right)^n(b_0-a_0)$ for every $n$ --- with equality.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[invariance]\label{thm:inv}
If $(a_0,b_0)$ encloses $S$ and $a_0<b_0$, then $(p_n,q_n)$ encloses $S$ for every $n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction. In the \texttt{true} branch $m_2$ is certified as an upper bound and the old lower witness is retained; in the \texttt{false} branch a member above $m_1$ is produced and the old upper bound is retained. The query points lie strictly inside, so $m_1<m_2$ and the datum applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[constructive least upper bound principle]\label{thm:lub}
Let $S$ be nonempty and bounded above with a located datum $L$ and an initial enclosure $(a_0,b_0)$, $a_0<b_0$. Then $S$ has a least upper bound $u$ and, for every $n$,
\[
p_n\le u\le q_n,\qquad q_n-p_n=\left(\tfrac23\right)^n(b_0-a_0).
\]
Moreover $u$ is a Bishop real: taking $n(k)$ to be the least stage with $\left(\frac23\right)^n(b_0-a_0)\le\frac1{k+1}$, the sequence $k\mapsto p_{n(k)}$ is a regular sequence of rationals denoting $u$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{example}
For $c\in\Q$ the half-line $S=(-\infty,c]$ has the located datum $L(p,q):=[\,c\le q\,]$, a decidable rational comparison. Running the trisection on $[0,1]$ with $c=1/2$ produces
\[
(0,1),\quad\Bigl(0,\tfrac23\Bigr),\quad\Bigl(\tfrac29,\tfrac23\Bigr),\quad\Bigl(\tfrac29,\tfrac{14}{27}\Bigr),\ \dots
\]
and after ten steps the width is exactly $(2/3)^{10}$, with $\tfrac12$ inside the enclosure.
\end{example}

\begin{theorem}[classical equivalence]
Assuming the classically valid decision ``is $q$ an upper bound of $S$?'', every $S$ has a located datum, namely $L(p,q):=[\,\forall s\in S,\ s\le q\,]$.
\end{theorem}

So the constructive principle is classically equivalent to ordinary completeness; its entire content is the extra datum.

\section{Optimising the located search}

\begin{algorithmx}[general one-query step]
Fix $0<\alpha<\beta<1$. Given $(p,q)$, query at $p+\alpha(q-p)$ and $p+\beta(q-p)$ and return
\[
T_{\alpha,\beta}(p,q)=\begin{cases}\bigl(p,\ p+\beta(q-p)\bigr)&\text{on \texttt{true}},\\ \bigl(p+\alpha(q-p),\ q\bigr)&\text{on \texttt{false}}.\end{cases}
\]
\end{algorithmx}

\begin{theorem}[exact contraction factor]\label{thm:gencontract}
For $0<\alpha<\beta<1$ the scheme $T_{\alpha,\beta}$ preserves the enclosure invariant, never degenerates, and after $n$ oracle calls
\[
q_n-p_n\;\le\;\bigl(\max(\beta,\,1-\alpha)\bigr)^n(b_0-a_0),
\]
the factor being attained in the worst case: the \texttt{true} branch contracts by $\beta$, the \texttt{false} branch by $1-\alpha$.
\end{theorem}

Trisection is $(\alpha,\beta)=(\frac13,\frac23)$, giving $\max(\frac23,\frac23)=\frac23$.

\begin{theorem}[trisection is not optimal]\label{thm:notopt}
The scheme with $(\alpha,\beta)=\bigl(\frac25,\frac12\bigr)$ preserves the same enclosure invariant and contracts by $\max\bigl(\frac12,\frac35\bigr)=\frac35<\frac23$ per oracle call.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[the optimal ratio is the unattained infimum $\tfrac12$]\label{thm:half}
\begin{enumerate}\renewcommand{\labelenumi}{(\roman{enumi})}
\item For all $\alpha<\beta$, $\max(\beta,1-\alpha)>\frac12$.
\item For every $\eta>0$ there are $0<\alpha<\beta<1$ with $\max(\beta,1-\alpha)<\frac12+\eta$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(i) If $\beta>\frac12$ we are done; if $\beta\le\frac12$ then $\alpha<\frac12$, so $1-\alpha>\frac12$. (ii) Put $t:=\min(\eta,\frac14)>0$, $\alpha:=\frac12-\frac t2$, $\beta:=\frac12+\frac t2$; then $\max(\beta,1-\alpha)=\frac12+\frac t2<\frac12+\eta$.
\end{proof}

The interpretation is information-theoretic: one oracle call returns one bit, and one bit at best halves the search space. The bound is not attained because the two query points must be \emph{distinct} --- the datum is only defined for $p<q$, and it is exactly the gap between the query points that gives the oracle freedom to answer either way. The constructive algorithm pays a strictly positive, arbitrarily small tax for the very ambiguity that makes locatedness implementable.

\section{Algorithmic summary}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{3.1cm}p{3.3cm}p{2.6cm}p{5.0cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Algorithm} & \textbf{Input} & \textbf{Output} & \textbf{Guarantee}\\
\midrule
Approximation & Bishop real $x$, target $\varepsilon$ & rational $x_n$ & $|\hat x-x_n|\le\varepsilon$ for $n=\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil$\\
Shifted diagonal & regular sequence of reals & Bishop real $L$ & $|\hat L-\hat x^{(k)}|\le\frac1{k+1}$\\
Cotransitivity test & certificate for $x<y$, third real $z$ & branch & one rational comparison at any $m$ with $\frac1{m+1}\le\frac g8$\\
Sign-change grid search & $f$ with modulus $\omega$, $N$ & grid index $k$ & $|f(\gr_k)|\le\varepsilon$ if mesh $\le\omega(\varepsilon)$; and $\gr_k$ within one mesh of a root\\
One-query located search & located datum, $(\alpha,\beta)$ & enclosure of $\sup S$ & width $\le\max(\beta,1-\alpha)^n(b_0-a_0)$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

In oracle/evaluation calls: the grid search at accuracy $\varepsilon$ costs $N+1$ evaluations with $N=\lceil(b-a)/\omega(\varepsilon)\rceil$, i.e.\ $O\bigl((b-a)c/\varepsilon\bigr)$ for $c$-Lipschitz $f$; the located search costs $\lceil\log(1/\varepsilon)/\log(1/\rho)\rceil$ oracle calls with $\rho=\max(\beta,1-\alpha)$, so improving $\rho$ from $2/3$ to $3/5$ is a speedup factor $\log(3/2)/\log(5/3)\approx0.794$, and $\rho\to1/2$ gives at best $\log(3/2)/\log2\approx0.585$.

The grid search is \emph{not} a bisection: bisection would require deciding the sign of $f$ at a midpoint, which is exactly the undecidable comparison. The linear scan avoids it because it only needs the finite set $\{k: f(\gr_k)\le0\}$ to have a maximum.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{A pattern: overlapping disjunctions}

Three central results share a shape. Cotransitivity concludes ``$x<z$ \emph{or} $z<y$''; constructive location concludes ``$a<x$ \emph{or} $x<b$''; the located datum concludes ``$q$ is an upper bound \emph{or} some member exceeds $p$''. In each case both branches may hold. The classical statement is an exclusive dichotomy that is undecidable; the constructive replacement is an \emph{overlapping} disjunction that is decidable. The overlap is the mechanism, not a defect, and the size of the slack is the quantitative content: $\frac g8$, $\frac{b-a}{4}$, $q-p$ respectively. Theorem~\ref{thm:half} says that the slack in the located datum forces a strictly positive information loss which can nonetheless be made arbitrarily small.

\subsection{Where the classical proofs hide their hypotheses}

Each constructive theorem has a classical counterpart with strictly fewer hypotheses, and in each case the missing hypothesis is one the classical proof consumes invisibly: a modulus for completeness (with the shift forced, Theorem~\ref{thm:shiftnec}); a modulus and either a weakened conclusion or a slope bound for the intermediate value theorem (the shelf family, Theorem~\ref{thm:brouwer}, shows this is not an artefact of technique); locatedness for the least upper bound principle, classically free. The uniform diagnosis: the classical proof performs an undecidable decision, and the constructive theorem either supplies that decision as data or weakens the conclusion until the decision is unnecessary.

\subsection{Sharpness as a dividend}

The sharpness results cannot even be \emph{stated} in a purely existential development. ``The constant $\varepsilon/c$ is attained'' presupposes a named constant; ``the shift $2n+1$ cannot be removed'' presupposes a formula; ``$2/3$ is not optimal'' presupposes an algorithm with a rate. Explicitness makes constructions criticisable, and the criticism yields new mathematics.

\subsection{Limitations}

Our metatheory is classical: we prove classical statements about constructive data, and use the classical intermediate value theorem to produce the exact root whose \emph{location} is then computed constructively. A fully intuitionistic treatment would construct the root by the search itself; this is a difference of packaging rather than of content, and the sharpness statements are most naturally classical anyway.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{conjecture}[$k$-query contraction]
Generalise the one-query step to $k$ oracle calls per step, at pairs $\bigl(p+\alpha_i(q-p),\,p+\beta_i(q-p)\bigr)$ with $\alpha_1<\beta_1\le\alpha_2<\beta_2\le\cdots<\beta_k$, keeping the smallest enclosure the answers certify. Then the worst-case contraction factor of any such scheme is $>\frac1{k+1}$, and for every $\eta>0$ some $k$-query scheme achieves a factor $<\frac1{k+1}+\eta$. In particular the per-oracle-call efficiency $(\text{contraction})^{1/k}$ tends to $0$ as $k\to\infty$: batching queries strictly pays.
\end{conjecture}

Falsifiable: a $k$-query scheme (for a concrete $k$, e.g.\ $k=2$) provably preserving the enclosure invariant and contracting by $\le\frac1{k+1}$ refutes the first half; a proof that no $2$-query scheme beats, say, $2/5$ refutes the second.

\begin{conjecture}[cotransitivity threshold]
The constant $6$ is optimal for Theorem~\ref{thm:cotrans}: the hypothesis $\frac{1}{m+1}\le\frac{g}{\kappa}$ with $\kappa<6$ is insufficient --- there are $x,y,z$ and indices $n,m$ satisfying it for which the midpoint test at $m$ decides neither $x<z$ nor $z<y$ --- while the conclusion of cotransitivity does hold under $\frac1{m+1}<\frac g6$.
\end{conjecture}

Falsifiable: a proof with $\kappa<6$ refutes the first half; an explicit triple defeating $6$ refutes the second.

\begin{conjecture}[multiplication bound]
Replacing $B(x)=\lceil|x_0|\rceil+2$ of Definition~\ref{def:bound} by $\lceil|x_0|\rceil+1$ still yields a regular sequence for the product, and the identification of the product with $\hat x\hat y$ continues to hold; the constant $1$ is then optimal, i.e.\ $\lceil|x_0|\rceil$ alone fails for some pair.
\end{conjecture}

Falsifiable: a pair $x,y$ for which the sequence defined with $\lceil|x_0|\rceil+1$ violates regularity refutes the first half; a proof that $\lceil|x_0|\rceil$ always suffices refutes the second.

\medskip
\noindent Further questions: is $n\mapsto2n+1$ the least shift for which the pointwise sum of two regular sequences is regular? Is $1$ the exact oscillation infimum in Theorem~\ref{thm:osc}, attained by the discontinuous selector? Can the whole of Theorem~\ref{thm:civt} be rederived from bracketing alone, with the slope bound entering only in the uniqueness statement?

\section{Conclusion}

We have carried out a quantitative development of Bishop's constructive analysis in which every existence statement carries an explicit modulus: real numbers as regular sequences with the canonical rate $1/(n+1)$; completeness by the shifted diagonal $n\mapsto x^{(2n+1)}_{2n+1}$, with the shift shown necessary; an order carrying certificates, with an explicit cotransitivity algorithm and a proof that the certificate cannot be bounded in advance; the intermediate value theorem in its approximate form (always available) and its exact form (available under a slope bound, with root modulus $\delta\mapsto\omega(c\delta)$ and the sharp displacement bound $\varepsilon/c$); a Brouwerian counterexample quantified to oscillation $\ge1$; a bracketing refinement showing that sign changes locate roots better than residuals do; and the least upper bound principle for located sets, with the exact rate $(2/3)^n$ improved to $\max(\beta,1-\alpha)^n$ and the optimal ratio identified as the unattained infimum $1/2$.

Once a rate is written down, one can ask whether it is optimal; once an algorithm is written down, one can ask whether it is efficient. Classical theorems, which assert only that something exists, do not admit these questions. Bishop's discipline turns analysis into a subject with constants --- and constants can be improved.

"""
Bishop's constructive analysis: numerical demonstrations.
==========================================================

Every real number here is a *regular sequence of rationals*: a function

    x : N -> Q      with      |x(m) - x(n)| <= 1/(m+1) + 1/(n+1).

The index IS the precision: |x_hat - x(n)| <= 1/(n+1), where x_hat is the
classical real denoted by x.  Everything below is exact rational arithmetic
(``fractions.Fraction``); no floating point enters the certified computations.

Demonstrations
--------------
  1. Explicit modulus: the n-th approximation is within 1/(n+1).
  2. Arithmetic with index shifts: sum, product, and a computable sqrt(2).
  3. Constructive completeness: the shifted diagonal, and the explicit family
     showing the unshifted diagonal fails regularity.
  4. The constructive order: witnessed comparison, cotransitivity by one
     rational test, and the impossibility of a uniform witness bound.
  5. The approximate intermediate value theorem by grid search, its exact
     form under a slope bound, and the sharpness of the constant eps/c.
  6. The Brouwerian counterexample: the shelf family's root jumps by 1.
  7. Bracketing beats bounding: the dip function defeats local non-constancy.
  8. Located sets: the trisection search, and the optimal one-query ratio.

Run with:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from fractions import Fraction as F
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple

Rat = F
RegSeq = Callable[[int], Rat]  # a Bishop real: n |-> n-th rational approximation


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Utilities
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def banner(title: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 74)


def err_bar(n: int) -> Rat:
    """The canonical accuracy attached to index n."""
    return F(1, n + 1)


def check_regular(x: RegSeq, upto: int = 40) -> bool:
    """Verify |x(m) - x(n)| <= 1/(m+1) + 1/(n+1) for all m, n <= upto."""
    return all(
        abs(x(m) - x(n)) <= err_bar(m) + err_bar(n)
        for m in range(upto + 1)
        for n in range(upto + 1)
    )


def isqrt(n: int) -> int:
    return math.isqrt(n)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Bishop reals and the explicit modulus
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def of_rat(q: Rat) -> RegSeq:
    """The Bishop real determined by a rational constant."""
    return lambda n: q


def sqrt_two(n: int) -> Rat:
    """floor(sqrt(2 (n+1)^2)) / (n+1):  an explicitly computable irrational."""
    m = n + 1
    return F(isqrt(2 * m * m), m)


def demo_explicit_modulus() -> None:
    banner("1.  EXPLICIT MODULUS:  |x_hat - x(n)| <= 1/(n+1)")
    print("  Bishop real: sqrt(2)_n = floor(sqrt(2(n+1)^2)) / (n+1)\n")
    print(f"  {'n':>7}  {'x(n)':>18}  {'|x_hat - x(n)|':>16}  {'1/(n+1)':>12}  ok")
    true_sqrt2 = F(math.isqrt(2 * 10**40), 10**20)  # 20 exact digits, as a rational
    for n in (0, 4, 9, 99, 999, 9999):
        v = sqrt_two(n)
        e = abs(true_sqrt2 - v)
        bound = err_bar(n)
        print(
            f"  {n:>7}  {str(v):>18}  {float(e):>16.3e}  "
            f"{float(bound):>12.3e}  {'YES' if e <= bound else 'NO'}"
        )
    print("\n  The index is the precision: no search, no waiting phase.")
    print(f"  Regularity verified for all m, n <= 40:  {check_regular(sqrt_two)}")
    print(f"  sqrt(2)_4  = {sqrt_two(4)}      (exactly 7/5)")
    print(f"  sqrt(2)_99 = {sqrt_two(99)}   (exactly 141/100)")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Arithmetic with index shifts
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def add(x: RegSeq, y: RegSeq) -> RegSeq:
    """(x + y)_n = x_{2n+1} + y_{2n+1}: Bishop's shift halves each error."""
    return lambda n: x(2 * n + 1) + y(2 * n + 1)


def canonical_bound(x: RegSeq) -> int:
    """B(x) = ceil(|x_0|) + 2 dominates every |x_n|."""
    return math.ceil(abs(x(0))) + 2


def mul(x: RegSeq, y: RegSeq) -> RegSeq:
    """(x*y)_n = x_{mu(n)} y_{mu(n)} with mu(n) = (B(x)+B(y))(n+1)."""
    M = canonical_bound(x) + canonical_bound(y)
    return lambda n: x(M * (n + 1)) * y(M * (n + 1))


def demo_arithmetic() -> None:
    banner("2.  ARITHMETIC WITH INDEX SHIFTS")
    s = add(sqrt_two, sqrt_two)
    p = mul(sqrt_two, sqrt_two)
    print("  x = sqrt(2) as a Bishop real.")
    print(f"  Canonical bound B(x) = ceil(|x_0|) + 2 = {canonical_bound(sqrt_two)}")
    print(f"  Product index shift  mu(n) = {2 * canonical_bound(sqrt_two)}(n+1)\n")
    print(f"  {'n':>6}  {'(x+x)(n)':>22}  {'err':>10}  {'(x*x)(n)':>22}  {'err':>10}")
    for n in (0, 2, 10, 100, 1000):
        sv, pv = s(n), p(n)
        print(
            f"  {n:>6}  {str(sv)[:22]:>22}  {float(abs(sv - 2 * math.sqrt(2))):>10.2e}"
            f"  {str(pv)[:22]:>22}  {float(abs(pv - 2)):>10.2e}"
        )
    print(f"\n  Sum regular (m,n <= 30):     {check_regular(s, 30)}")
    print(f"  Product regular (m,n <= 30): {check_regular(p, 30)}")
    print("  The shift is proportional to the magnitudes: larger factors need")
    print("  more digits before their product is trustworthy.")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Constructive completeness and the necessity of the diagonal shift
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def witness_family(k: int) -> RegSeq:
    """w^(k)_n = 1/(k+1) + (-1)^k / (n+1).  Denotes 1/(k+1)."""
    sign = 1 if k % 2 == 0 else -1
    return lambda n: F(1, k + 1) + sign * F(1, n + 1)


def shifted_diagonal(family: Callable[[int], RegSeq]) -> RegSeq:
    """Bishop's limit: L_n = x^(2n+1)_{2n+1}."""
    return lambda n: family(2 * n + 1)(2 * n + 1)


def unshifted_diagonal(family: Callable[[int], RegSeq]) -> RegSeq:
    """The naive candidate: L_n = x^(n)_n.  Not regular in general."""
    return lambda n: family(n)(n)

# 4. The constructive order
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def find_lt_witness(x: RegSeq, y: RegSeq, max_n: int = 100000) -> int | None:
    """A witness n with x(n) + 2/(n+1) < y(n): a certificate for x < y."""
    n = 0
    while n <= max_n:
        if x(n) + 2 * err_bar(n) < y(n):
            return n
        n = 2 * n + 1
    return None


def cotransitivity_test(
    x: RegSeq, y: RegSeq, z: RegSeq, n: int
) -> Tuple[int, Rat, str]:
    """
    Given a witness n for x < y with certified gap g = y_n - x_n - 2/(n+1),
    choose any m with 1/(m+1) <= g/8 and make ONE rational comparison of z_m
    against the midpoint.  Returns (m, g, branch).
    """
    g = y(n) - x(n) - 2 * err_bar(n)
    assert g > 0, "n is not a witness"
    m = max(0, math.ceil(8 / g) - 1)  # smallest m with 1/(m+1) <= g/8
    branch = "x < z" if z(m) >= (x(m) + y(m)) / 2 else "z < y"
    return m, g, branch

# 5. The intermediate value theorem

def grid_search(
    f: Callable[[float], float], a: float, b: float, N: int
) -> Tuple[int, float, float]:
    """
    The sign-change search: return the LARGEST index k with f(grid_k) <= 0,
    together with the grid point and the value there.  Cost: N+1 evaluations.
    """
    step = (b - a) / N
    best = 0
    for k in range(N + 1):
        if f(a + k * step) <= 0:
            best = k
    return best, a + best * step, f(a + best * step)

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def shelf(t: float, x: float) -> float:
    """shelf_t(x) = min(x - 1, max(t, x - 2)) on [0,3]: 1-Lipschitz in x."""
    return min(x - 1.0, max(t, x - 2.0))


def shelf_exact_root(t: float) -> float:
    """The forced root: 1 for t > 0, 2 for t < 0, anywhere in [1,2] for t = 0."""
    if t > 0:
        return 1.0
    if t < 0:
        return 2.0
    return float("nan")

def dip(eta: float, x: float) -> float:
    """dip_eta(x) = min(x - 1, |x - 3| + eta): unique root 1, tiny dip at 3."""
    return min(x - 1.0, abs(x - 3.0) + eta)

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 8. Located sets: the supremum search and its optimal contraction
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def trisection(
    L: Callable[[Rat, Rat], bool], a0: Rat, b0: Rat, steps: int
) -> List[Tuple[Rat, Rat]]:
    """Bishop's trisection search.  Width shrinks by EXACTLY 2/3 per step."""
    out = [(a0, b0)]
    p, q = a0, b0
    for _ in range(steps):
        m1 = p + (q - p) / 3
        m2 = p + 2 * (q - p) / 3
        p, q = (p, m2) if L(m1, m2) else (m1, q)
        out.append((p, q))
    return out


def one_query_search(
    alpha: Rat, beta: Rat, L: Callable[[Rat, Rat], bool], a0: Rat, b0: Rat, steps: int
) -> List[Tuple[Rat, Rat]]:
    """General one-query search: contraction factor exactly max(beta, 1-alpha)."""
    out = [(a0, b0)]
    p, q = a0, b0
    for _ in range(steps):
        qa = p + alpha * (q - p)
        qb = p + beta * (q - p)
        p, q = (p, qb) if L(qa, qb) else (qa, q)
        out.append((p, q))
    return out

    print("\n  Width is EXACTLY (2/3)^n -- not merely bounded by it.\n")

    schemes = [

import math
from fractions import Fraction as F
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple

Rat = F
RegSeq = Callable[[int], Rat]  # a Bishop real: n |-> n-th rational approximation

# 0. Utilities
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def banner(title: str) -> None:

    print(title)

def err_bar(n: int) -> Rat:
    """The canonical accuracy attached to index n."""
    return F(1, n + 1)


def check_regular(x: RegSeq, upto: int = 40) -> bool:
    """Verify |x(m) - x(n)| <= 1/(m+1) + 1/(n+1) for all m, n <= upto."""
    return all(
        abs(x(m) - x(n)) <= err_bar(m) + err_bar(n)
        for m in range(upto + 1)
        for n in range(upto + 1)
    )


def isqrt(n: int) -> int:
    return math.isqrt(n)

# 1. Bishop reals and the explicit modulus
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def of_rat(q: Rat) -> RegSeq:
    """The Bishop real determined by a rational constant."""
    return lambda n: q


def sqrt_two(n: int) -> Rat:
    """floor(sqrt(2 (n+1)^2)) / (n+1):  an explicitly computable irrational."""
    m = n + 1
    return F(isqrt(2 * m * m), m)

# 2. Arithmetic with index shifts

def add(x: RegSeq, y: RegSeq) -> RegSeq:
    """(x + y)_n = x_{2n+1} + y_{2n+1}: Bishop's shift halves each error."""
    return lambda n: x(2 * n + 1) + y(2 * n + 1)


def canonical_bound(x: RegSeq) -> int:
    """B(x) = ceil(|x_0|) + 2 dominates every |x_n|."""
    return math.ceil(abs(x(0))) + 2


def mul(x: RegSeq, y: RegSeq) -> RegSeq:
    """(x*y)_n = x_{mu(n)} y_{mu(n)} with mu(n) = (B(x)+B(y))(n+1)."""
    M = canonical_bound(x) + canonical_bound(y)
    return lambda n: x(M * (n + 1)) * y(M * (n + 1))

# 3. Constructive completeness and the necessity of the diagonal shift
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def witness_family(k: int) -> RegSeq:
    """w^(k)_n = 1/(k+1) + (-1)^k / (n+1).  Denotes 1/(k+1)."""
    sign = 1 if k % 2 == 0 else -1
    return lambda n: F(1, k + 1) + sign * F(1, n + 1)


def shifted_diagonal(family: Callable[[int], RegSeq]) -> RegSeq:
    """Bishop's limit: L_n = x^(2n+1)_{2n+1}."""
    return lambda n: family(2 * n + 1)(2 * n + 1)


def unshifted_diagonal(family: Callable[[int], RegSeq]) -> RegSeq:
    """The naive candidate: L_n = x^(n)_n.  Not regular in general."""
    return lambda n: family(n)(n)

def find_lt_witness(x: RegSeq, y: RegSeq, max_n: int = 100000) -> int | None:
    """A witness n with x(n) + 2/(n+1) < y(n): a certificate for x < y."""
    n = 0
    while n <= max_n:
        if x(n) + 2 * err_bar(n) < y(n):
            return n
        n = 2 * n + 1
    return None


def cotransitivity_test(
    x: RegSeq, y: RegSeq, z: RegSeq, n: int
) -> Tuple[int, Rat, str]:
    """
    Given a witness n for x < y with certified gap g = y_n - x_n - 2/(n+1),
    choose any m with 1/(m+1) <= g/8 and make ONE rational comparison of z_m
    against the midpoint.  Returns (m, g, branch).
    """
    g = y(n) - x(n) - 2 * err_bar(n)
    assert g > 0, "n is not a witness"
    m = max(0, math.ceil(8 / g) - 1)  # smallest m with 1/(m+1) <= g/8
    branch = "x < z" if z(m) >= (x(m) + y(m)) / 2 else "z < y"
    return m, g, branch

def grid_search(
    f: Callable[[float], float], a: float, b: float, N: int
) -> Tuple[int, float, float]:
    """
    The sign-change search: return the LARGEST index k with f(grid_k) <= 0,
    together with the grid point and the value there.  Cost: N+1 evaluations.
    """
    step = (b - a) / N
    best = 0
    for k in range(N + 1):
        if f(a + k * step) <= 0:
            best = k
    return best, a + best * step, f(a + best * step)

def shelf(t: float, x: float) -> float:
    """shelf_t(x) = min(x - 1, max(t, x - 2)) on [0,3]: 1-Lipschitz in x."""
    return min(x - 1.0, max(t, x - 2.0))


def shelf_exact_root(t: float) -> float:
    """The forced root: 1 for t > 0, 2 for t < 0, anywhere in [1,2] for t = 0."""
    if t > 0:
        return 1.0
    if t < 0:
        return 2.0
    return float("nan")

    """dip_eta(x) = min(x - 1, |x - 3| + eta): unique root 1, tiny dip at 3."""

# 8. Located sets: the supremum search and its optimal contraction

def trisection(
    L: Callable[[Rat, Rat], bool], a0: Rat, b0: Rat, steps: int
) -> List[Tuple[Rat, Rat]]:
    """Bishop's trisection search.  Width shrinks by EXACTLY 2/3 per step."""
    out = [(a0, b0)]
    p, q = a0, b0
    for _ in range(steps):
        m1 = p + (q - p) / 3
        m2 = p + 2 * (q - p) / 3
        p, q = (p, m2) if L(m1, m2) else (m1, q)
        out.append((p, q))
    return out


def one_query_search(
    alpha: Rat, beta: Rat, L: Callable[[Rat, Rat], bool], a0: Rat, b0: Rat, steps: int
) -> List[Tuple[Rat, Rat]]:
    """General one-query search: contraction factor exactly max(beta, 1-alpha)."""
    out = [(a0, b0)]
    p, q = a0, b0
    for _ in range(steps):
        qa = p + alpha * (q - p)
        qb = p + beta * (q - p)
        p, q = (p, qb) if L(qa, qb) else (qa, q)
        out.append((p, q))
    return out

    print("\n  Width is EXACTLY (2/3)^n -- not merely bounded by it.\n")

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from fractions import Fraction as F
from typing import Callable


class BishopReal:
    """A regular sequence of rationals, with certified arithmetic."""

    __slots__ = ("approx", "name")

    def __init__(self, approx: Callable[[int], F], name: str = "x") -> None:
        self.approx = approx
        self.name = name

    def __call__(self, n: int) -> F:
        return self.approx(n)

    # ---- certification -------------------------------------------------

    def check_regular(self, upto: int = 30) -> bool:
        """Verify the defining inequality on all indices up to `upto`."""
        return all(
            abs(self(m) - self(n)) <= F(1, m + 1) + F(1, n + 1)
            for m in range(upto + 1)
            for n in range(upto + 1)
        )

    def to_accuracy(self, eps: F) -> F:
        """Return a rational within `eps` of the denoted real. O(1) queries."""
        n = max(0, math.ceil(1 / eps) - 1)
        return self(n)

    # ---- the canonical bound used by multiplication ---------------------

    def bound(self) -> int:
        """B(x) = ceil(|x_0|) + 2 dominates every |x_n|."""
        return math.ceil(abs(self(0))) + 2

    # ---- operations, each with its index shift --------------------------

    def __neg__(self) -> "BishopReal":
        return BishopReal(lambda n: -self(n), f"-{self.name}")

    def __add__(self, other: "BishopReal") -> "BishopReal":
        """Shift n -> 2n+1: two errors of 1/(2n+2) sum to the allowance."""
        return BishopReal(
            lambda n: self(2 * n + 1) + other(2 * n + 1),
            f"({self.name}+{other.name})",
        )

    def __sub__(self, other: "BishopReal") -> "BishopReal":
        return self + (-other)

    def __mul__(self, other: "BishopReal") -> "BishopReal":
        """Shift n -> M(n+1) with M = B(x) + B(y): errors scale with size."""
        M = self.bound() + other.bound()
        return BishopReal(
            lambda n: self(M * (n + 1)) * other(M * (n + 1)),
            f"({self.name}*{other.name})",
        )

    # ---- the constructive order ----------------------------------------

    def lt_witness(self, other: "BishopReal", max_n: int = 1 << 24) -> int | None:
        """
        Search for a certificate n with x(n) + 2/(n+1) < y(n), proving x < y.
        Doubling search: O(log n*) queries for the least witness magnitude.
        """
        n = 0
        while n <= max_n:
            if self(n) + 2 * F(1, n + 1) < other(n):
                return n
            n = 2 * n + 1
        return None


def rational(q: F) -> BishopReal:
    return BishopReal(lambda n: q, str(q))


def sqrt_of(k: int) -> BishopReal:
    """The computable Bishop real denoting sqrt(k), via integer square roots."""

    def approx(n: int) -> F:
        m = n + 1
        return F(math.isqrt(k * m * m), m)

    return BishopReal(approx, f"sqrt({k})")

import math
from typing import Callable, NamedTuple, Optional


class SearchResult(NamedTuple):
    index: int
    point: float
    value: float
    mesh: float
    bracket: Optional[tuple[float, float]]  # (grid_k, grid_{k+1}), if any
    evaluations: int


def sign_change_grid_search(
    f: Callable[[float], float], a: float, b: float, N: int
) -> SearchResult:
    """Return the largest grid index k with f(grid_k) <= 0, and its bracket."""
    if N < 1:
        raise ValueError("N must be at least 1")
    if f(a) > 0 or f(b) < 0:
        raise ValueError("the sign condition f(a) <= 0 <= f(b) fails")
    mesh = (b - a) / N
    best = 0
    for k in range(N + 1):
        if f(a + k * mesh) <= 0.0:
            best = k
    point = a + best * mesh
    bracket = None if best == N else (point, point + mesh)
    return SearchResult(best, point, f(point), mesh, bracket, N + 1)

    f: Callable[[float], float],

    b: float,
    omega: Callable[[float], float],

    N = max(1, math.ceil((b - a) / omega(eps)))

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from fractions import Fraction as F
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple

Oracle = Callable[[F, F], bool]


def contraction_ratio(alpha: F, beta: F) -> F:
    """The exact worst-case contraction factor of the (alpha, beta) scheme."""
    if not (0 < alpha < beta < 1):
        raise ValueError("require 0 < alpha < beta < 1")
    return max(beta, 1 - alpha)


def located_search(
    oracle: Oracle, a0: F, b0: F, alpha: F = F(1, 3), beta: F = F(2, 3), steps: int = 20
) -> List[Tuple[F, F]]:
    """Run the one-query search, returning the full list of enclosures."""
    contraction_ratio(alpha, beta)  # validates the parameters
    out = [(a0, b0)]
    p, q = a0, b0
    for _ in range(steps):
        qa = p + alpha * (q - p)
        qb = p + beta * (q - p)
        p, q = (p, qb) if oracle(qa, qb) else (qa, q)
        out.append((p, q))
    return out


def steps_for_accuracy(alpha: F, beta: F, width0: F, eps: F) -> int:
    """Number of oracle calls needed to reach an enclosure of width <= eps."""
    rho = float(contraction_ratio(alpha, beta))
    return max(0, math.ceil(math.log(float(eps / width0)) / math.log(rho)))


def sup_as_regular_sequence(
    oracle: Oracle, a0: F, b0: F, alpha: F = F(1, 3), beta: F = F(2, 3)
) -> Callable[[int], F]:
    """
    Present sup S as a Bishop real: the k-th term is the left endpoint of the
    first enclosure narrower than 1/(k+1).
    """

    def approx(k: int) -> F:
        target = F(1, k + 1)
        n = steps_for_accuracy(alpha, beta, b0 - a0, target)
        return located_search(oracle, a0, b0, alpha, beta, n)[-1][0]

    return approx


def near_optimal_scheme(eta: F) -> Tuple[F, F]:
    """A one-query scheme with contraction ratio below 1/2 + eta."""
    t = min(eta, F(1, 4))
    return F(1, 2) - t / 2, F(1, 2) + t / 2

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from fractions import Fraction as F
from typing import Callable, NamedTuple, Optional

RegSeq = Callable[[int], F]


class Decision(NamedTuple):
    branch: str            # "x < z" or "z < y"
    test_index: int        # the index m at which the single comparison was made
    gap: F                 # the certified rational gap g
    certificate: str       # the rational inequality proving the branch


def certified_gap(x: RegSeq, y: RegSeq, n: int) -> F:
    """The rational lower bound on y_hat - x_hat read off from the witness n."""
    g = y(n) - x(n) - 2 * F(1, n + 1)
    if g <= 0:
        raise ValueError(f"index {n} is not a witness for x < y")
    return g


def refinement_index(g: F, kappa: int = 8) -> int:
    """The least m with 1/(m+1) <= g/kappa."""
    return max(0, math.ceil(kappa / g) - 1)


def cotransitivity(x: RegSeq, y: RegSeq, z: RegSeq, n: int) -> Decision:
    """Decide 'x < z' or 'z < y' by a single rational comparison."""
    g = certified_gap(x, y, n)
    m = refinement_index(g)
    midpoint = (x(m) + y(m)) / 2
    margin = 2 * F(1, m + 1)
    if z(m) >= midpoint:
        cert = f"x({m}) + 2/({m}+1) = {x(m) + margin} < {z(m)} = z({m})"
        assert x(m) + margin < z(m), "internal error: certificate invalid"
        return Decision("x < z", m, g, cert)
    cert = f"z({m}) + 2/({m}+1) = {z(m) + margin} < {y(m)} = y({m})"
    assert z(m) + margin < y(m), "internal error: certificate invalid"
    return Decision("z < y", m, g, cert)


def locate(x: RegSeq, a: F, b: F) -> tuple[str, int]:
    """
    Constructive location: for rationals a < b decide 'a < x' or 'x < b'
    by one comparison at any index n with 4/(n+1) <= b - a.
    """
    if a >= b:
        raise ValueError("require a < b")
    n = max(0, math.ceil(4 / (b - a)) - 1)
    return ("a < x" if x(n) >= (a + b) / 2 else "x < b"), n


def find_witness(x: RegSeq, y: RegSeq, max_n: int = 1 << 24) -> Optional[int]:
    n = 0
    while n <= max_n:
        if x(n) + 2 * F(1, n + 1) < y(n):
            return n
        n = 2 * n + 1
    return None

from __future__ import annotations

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def shelf(t: float, x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    return np.minimum(x - 1.0, np.maximum(t, x - 2.0))


def exact_root(t: float) -> float:
    return 1.0 if t > 0 else (2.0 if t < 0 else float("nan"))


def grid_approx_root(t: float, N: int) -> float:
    xs = np.linspace(0.0, 3.0, N + 1)
    vals = shelf(t, xs)
    k = int(np.max(np.nonzero(vals <= 0.0)[0]))
    return float(xs[k])

import math
from fractions import Fraction as F

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def sqrt_two(n: int) -> F:
    m = n + 1
    return F(math.isqrt(2 * m * m), m)


def w(k: int, n: int) -> F:
    return F(1, k + 1) + (1 if k % 2 == 0 else -1) * F(1, n + 1)


def main() -> None:
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))

    ns = np.arange(0, 400)
    true = math.sqrt(2)

    env = 1.0 / (ns + 1.0)

    ax1.semilogy(ns + 1, env, color="crimson", lw=2.2,
                 label=r"guaranteed envelope $1/(n+1)$")
    ax1.semilogy(ns + 1, np.maximum(errs, 1e-18), ".", ms=3.5, color="steelblue",

    ax1.set_xlabel("$n+1$")
    ax1.set_ylabel("error")

    ax2.plot(ks, unshifted, "o-", color="crimson", ms=6, lw=2,

    ax2.text(1.15, 1.05, "gap $=2$, but regularity\nallows only $3/2$",

    ax2.set_xlabel("index $n$")
    ax2.set_ylabel("value")
    ax2.set_title("Why the completeness theorem needs the shift $n\\mapsto 2n+1$")

/* ---------- exact rational arithmetic ---------- */
function gcd(a,b){a=a<0n?-a:a;b=b<0n?-b:b;while(b){[a,b]=[b,a%b];}return a;}
function Q(n,d){ n=BigInt(n); d=BigInt(d===undefined?1:d);
  if(d<0n){n=-n;d=-d;} const g=gcd(n,d)||1n; return {n:n/g,d:d/g}; }
const add=(a,b)=>Q(a.n*b.d+b.n*a.d,a.d*b.d);
const sub=(a,b)=>Q(a.n*b.d-b.n*a.d,a.d*b.d);
const mul=(a,b)=>Q(a.n*b.n,a.d*b.d);
const divq=(a,b)=>Q(a.n*b.d,a.d*b.n);
const cmp=(a,b)=>{const l=a.n*b.d,r=b.n*a.d;return l<r?-1:(l>r?1:0);};
const absq=a=>Q(a.n<0n?-a.n:a.n,a.d);
const num=a=>Number(a.n)/Number(a.d);
const str=a=>a.d===1n?a.n.toString():a.n+"/"+a.d;
function isqrt(v){ if(v<2n) return v; let x=v, y=(x+1n)/2n;
  while(y<x){x=y;y=(x+v/x)/2n;} return x; }

/* ---------- Bishop reals ---------- */
const REALS = {
  sqrt2:{f:n=>{const m=BigInt(n)+1n;return Q(isqrt(2n*m*m),m);}, name:"\u221A2", ref:Math.SQRT2},
  sqrt3:{f:n=>{const m=BigInt(n)+1n;return Q(isqrt(3n*m*m),m);}, name:"\u221A3", ref:Math.sqrt(3)},
  third:{f:n=>Q(1,3), name:"1/3", ref:1/3},
  wobble:{f:n=>add(Q(1),Q((n%2==0)?1:-1,n+1)), name:"wobbler", ref:1}
};
const bar = n => Q(1,n+1);

function regularUpTo(f,N){
  for(let m=0;m<=N;m++) for(let n=0;n<=N;n++)
    if(cmp(absq(sub(f(m),f(n))), add(bar(m),bar(n)))>0) return [false,m,n];
  return [true,0,0];
}
function boundOf(f){ const a=absq(f(0)); return Number((a.n+a.d-1n)/a.d)+2; }
function addSeq(f,g,shift){ return n => shift ? add(f(2*n+1),g(2*n+1)) : add(f(n),g(n)); }
function mulSeq(f,g,shift){ const M=boundOf(f)+boundOf(g);

    `mesh 3/N = ${res.mesh.toFixed(5)}<br>`+
    `search answer: k = ${res.k}, x = ${res.x.toFixed(5)}<br>`+

/* exact rationals over BigInt */
function gcd(a,b){a=a<0n?-a:a;b=b<0n?-b:b;while(b){[a,b]=[b,a%b];}return a;}
function Q(n,d){n=BigInt(n);d=BigInt(d===undefined?1:d);
  if(d<0n){n=-n;d=-d;}const g=gcd(n,d)||1n;return{n:n/g,d:d/g};}
const add=(a,b)=>Q(a.n*b.d+b.n*a.d,a.d*b.d), sub=(a,b)=>Q(a.n*b.d-b.n*a.d,a.d*b.d);
const mul=(a,b)=>Q(a.n*b.n,a.d*b.d);
const cmp=(a,b)=>{const l=a.n*b.d,r=b.n*a.d;return l<r?-1:(l>r?1:0);};
const num=a=>Number(a.n)/Number(a.d);
const shortStr=a=>{const s=a.n+"/"+a.d;return s.length>18?num(a).toFixed(9):(a.d===1n?a.n.toString():s);};

function run(alpha,beta,c,steps){
  const out=[{p:Q(0),q:Q(1),qa:null,qb:null,ans:null}];
  let p=Q(0),q=Q(1);
  for(let i=0;i<steps;i++){
    const w=sub(q,p);
    const qa=add(p,mul(alpha,w)), qb=add(p,mul(beta,w));
    const ans = cmp(c,qb)<=0;            // located datum for S = (-inf, c]
    if(ans){ out.push({p:p,q:qb,qa:qa,qb:qb,ans:true}); q=qb; }
    else   { out.push({p:qa,q:q,qa:qa,qb:qb,ans:false}); p=qa; }
  }
  return out;
}

function fit(cv,h){const r=cv.getBoundingClientRect();
  cv.width=r.width*devicePixelRatio;cv.height=h*devicePixelRatio;

const g=id=>document.getElementById(id);

  const C=+g("c").value/1000, S=+g("steps").value;
  g("al").textContent=A.toFixed(3); g("be").textContent=B.toFixed(3);
  g("cl").textContent=C.toFixed(3); g("sl").textContent=S;
  const bad = !(A<B);
  g("warn").textContent = bad ? "need α < β : the two query points must be distinct." : "";
  if(bad) return;

  const alpha=Q(Math.round(A*1000),1000), beta=Q(Math.round(B*1000),1000),

  const rho=Math.max(B,1-A);

  /* enclosure ladder */
  const cv=g("cv"), ctx=cv.getContext("2d");
  const [W,H]=fit(cv,330), L=44,R=18,T=14,Bm=28;
  ctx.clearRect(0,0,W,H);
  const X=x=>L+(W-L-R)*x, rowH=(H-T-Bm)/Math.max(seq.length,1);
  for(let i=0;i<seq.length;i++){
    const y=T+i*rowH+rowH/2, s=seq[i];
    ctx.strokeStyle="#26304a"; ctx.lineWidth=1;
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(L,y); ctx.lineTo(W-R,y); ctx.stroke();
    const p=num(s.p), q=num(s.q);
    ctx.strokeStyle = s.ans===null?"#7aa7ff":(s.ans?"#67d4a8":"#ffb454");
    ctx.lineWidth=Math.max(3,Math.min(9,rowH*0.55));
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(X(p),y); ctx.lineTo(X(q),y); ctx.stroke();
    if(s.qa!==null){
      ctx.fillStyle="#e8ecf580";
      for(const t of [num(s.qa),num(s.qb)]){ctx.fillRect(X(t)-1,y-rowH*0.42,2,rowH*0.84);}
    }
    ctx.fillStyle="#67d4a8";
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(X(C),y,2.4,0,7); ctx.fill();
  }
  ctx.fillStyle="#95a1bb"; ctx.font="11px ui-monospace,monospace";
  ctx.fillText("0",L-8,H-12); ctx.fillText("1",W-R-4,H-12);
  ctx.fillStyle="#67d4a8"; ctx.fillText("c",X(C)-3,H-12);

  /* decay */
  const cv2=g("cv2"), c2=cv2.getContext("2d");
  const [W2,H2]=fit(cv2,200), L2=42,R2=12,T2=12,B2=26;
  c2.clearRect(0,0,W2,H2);
  const nmax=Math.max(S,20), ymin=Math.log10(Math.pow(Math.min(rho,0.5),nmax))-0.5;
  const PX=n=>L2+(W2-L2-R2)*n/nmax, PY=v=>T2+(H2-T2-B2)*(0-Math.log10(v))/(0-ymin);
  c2.strokeStyle="#36406080"; c2.beginPath();
  c2.moveTo(L2,T2);c2.lineTo(L2,H2-B2);c2.lineTo(W2-R2,H2-B2);c2.stroke();
  c2.strokeStyle="#4a5578"; c2.setLineDash([3,3]); c2.beginPath();
  for(let n=0;n<=nmax;n++){const v=Math.pow(0.5,n);(n?c2.lineTo:c2.moveTo).call(c2,PX(n),PY(Math.max(v,1e-30)));}
  c2.stroke(); c2.setLineDash([]);
  c2.strokeStyle="#ffb454"; c2.lineWidth=2.4; c2.beginPath();
  for(let n=0;n<=nmax;n++){const v=Math.pow(rho,n);(n?c2.lineTo:c2.moveTo).call(c2,PX(n),PY(Math.max(v,1e-30)));}
  c2.stroke();
  c2.strokeStyle="#67d4a8"; c2.lineWidth=1.6; c2.beginPath();
  for(let i=0;i<seq.length;i++){const w=Math.max(num(sub(seq[i].q,seq[i].p)),1e-30);
    (i?c2.lineTo:c2.moveTo).call(c2,PX(i),PY(w));}
  c2.stroke();
  c2.fillStyle="#95a1bb"; c2.font="11px ui-monospace,monospace";
  c2.fillText("oracle calls",(L2+W2)/2-30,H2-8);
  c2.fillStyle="#4a5578"; c2.fillText("2⁻ⁿ", PX(nmax)-24, PY(Math.pow(0.5,nmax))-4);

  /* stats */
  const w=num(sub(seq[seq.length-1].q,seq[seq.length-1].p));
  const calls=Math.ceil(Math.log(1e-12)/Math.log(rho));
  const callsTri=Math.ceil(Math.log(1e-12)/Math.log(2/3));
  g("stats").innerHTML =
    `<span class="badge">contraction</span> ρ = max(β, 1−α) = `+
    `<span class="hl">${rho.toFixed(6)}</span> `+
    `${rho>0.5?'<span class="ok">> 1/2 ✓</span>':'<span class="no">impossible</span>'}<br>`+
    `<span class="badge">width</span> after ${S} calls: ${w.toExponential(4)}<br>`+
    `<span class="badge">cost</span> ${calls} calls to reach 10⁻¹² `+
    `(trisection needs ${callsTri}; speedup ×${(callsTri/calls).toFixed(3)})<br>`+
    `<span class="badge">invariant</span> ${cmp(seq[seq.length-1].p,c)<0 && cmp(c,seq[seq.length-1].q)<=0
      ? '<span class="ok">c enclosed at every stage ✓</span>'
      : '<span class="no">violated</span>'}`;

  /* table */
  let h="<tr><th>n</th><th>p<sub>n</sub></th><th>q<sub>n</sub></th><th>width</th><th>answer</th></tr>";
  for(let i=0;i<Math.min(seq.length,20);i++){const s=seq[i];
    h+=`<tr><td>${i}</td><td class="mono">${shortStr(s.p)}</td>`+
       `<td class="mono">${shortStr(s.q)}</td>`+
       `<td class="mono">${num(sub(s.q,s.p)).toExponential(3)}</td>`+
       `<td class="${s.ans===null?'':(s.ans?'ok':'hl')}">${s.ans===null?'—':(s.ans?'true':'false')}</td></tr>`;}
  g("tab").innerHTML=h;
}
for(const id of ["alpha","beta","c","steps"]) g(id).addEventListener("input",draw);
for(const b of document.querySelectorAll("button[data-a]"))
  b.onclick=()=>{g("alpha").value=b.dataset.a; g("beta").value=b.dataset.b; draw();};
window.addEventListener("resize",draw);
draw();
</script>
