\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} box-counting dimension, Cantor space, fractal dimension, formal theories, counting complexity, asymptotic density, information rate, compressibility.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{Motivation}

How large is a body of mathematics? Cardinality is useless: any recursively axiomatised theory with a single free variable already proves countably many distinct statements, so all interesting theories are equinumerous. Deductive strength is the classical answer, but it is an \emph{order}, not a \emph{number}: consistency strength compares theories, it does not measure them on a scale.

There is a third answer, and it is quantitative. Fix an encoding of statements as finite bit strings. At each description length $n$ there are $2^n$ candidate strings, of which a theory accepts some sub-collection. The \emph{rate} at which that sub-collection grows --- the exponent $d$ such that roughly $2^{dn}$ strings of length $n$ are accepted --- is a single real number in $[0,1]$ capturing how much of the available description space the theory occupies. It is invariant under any re-encoding preserving lengths up to $o(n)$, monotone under enlarging the theory, and, as we show, possesses a complete and constructive realisation theory.

The exponent is not an ad hoc invention. It is precisely the box-counting dimension of the theory viewed as a subset of Cantor space $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ with the ultrametric $d(x,y)=2^{-\min\{i\,:\,x_i\ne y_i\}}$. Under that metric the closed balls of radius $2^{-n}$ are exactly the cylinders determined by the first $n$ coordinates, and the number needed to cover the set of infinite extensions of the theory's length-$n$ strings is exactly $|T_n|$. The box-counting formula $\log N(\varepsilon)/\log(1/\varepsilon)$ at $\varepsilon=2^{-n}$ reads $\log_2|T_n|/n$. The ``growth rate of truth'' and ``the fractal dimension of truth'' are literally the same quantity.

\subsection{The question addressed}

A prior development established that one specific theory --- a ``half-information'' theory in which odd-indexed coordinates are forced to zero --- has dimension exactly $1/2$. Is $1/2$ a distinguished value, an artefact of a symmetric construction, or the tip of a general law? We show it is the latter, in the strongest form: the dimension of a periodically constrained theory is \emph{exactly} the asymptotic density of its free coordinates, and by tuning that density every rational value in $[0,1]$ is realised by a concrete theory.

\subsection{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Framework and universal bounds: $0\le\dimT T\le 1$ for all $T$ (\S\ref{sec:bounds}).
\item Monotonicity: $T_n\subseteq T'_n$ for all $n$ implies $\dimT T\le\dimT T'$ (\S\ref{sec:mono}).
\item Exact combinatorics of periodic density theories: counting law, period relation, sandwich (\S\ref{sec:comb}).
\item The Density Theorem $\dimT D(m,R)=|R|/m$, with $O(1/n)$ convergence (\S\ref{sec:density}).
\item The Realisation Theorem: every rational in $[0,1]$ is a dimension (\S\ref{sec:spectrum}).
\item Exact algorithms with certified error bars (\S\ref{sec:algorithms}).
\item Interpretation and extensions (\S\ref{sec:interp}--\S\ref{sec:future}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{The framework}

\begin{definition}[Statement]
A \emph{statement of length $n$} is an element of $\{0,1\}^n$, i.e.\ a function $\{0,\dots,n-1\}\to\{0,1\}$, regarded as the encoding of a formal assertion under a fixed injective, length-respecting encoding scheme.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Theory]
A \emph{theory} is a family $T=(T_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ where each $T_n$ is a finite subset of $\{0,1\}^n$, the \emph{level $n$} of the theory. No deductive closure is imposed: $T$ is any length-graded set of accepted strings, modelling the theorems of an axiomatic system, the outputs of a decision procedure, a set of valid certificates, or an arbitrary language.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Count]
$\count(T,n):=|T_n|$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Trivial count bound]\label{lem:trivial}
For every theory $T$ and every $n$, $\count(T,n)\le 2^n$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
$T_n$ is a subset of a set of size $2^n$, and cardinality is monotone under inclusion.
\end{proof}

\begin{convention}\label{conv:log0}
Throughout, $\log_2 0:=0$. This is the real logarithm extended by $0$ at $0$; it makes an empty level contribute the minimal possible finite-scale estimate.
\end{convention}

\begin{definition}[Finite-scale estimate]
For $n\ge 1$, $\ \delta_T(n):=\dfrac{\log_2\count(T,n)}{n}$. (At $n=0$ the expression is interpreted as $0$; a single index is irrelevant to the asymptotics.)
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Fractal dimension of a theory]
$\displaystyle \dimT T:=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\delta_T(n)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2|T_n|}{n}.$
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}[Why this is a box dimension]
Let $[T]\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ be the set of infinite sequences all of whose length-$n$ prefixes lie in $T_n$. With the ultrametric above, the minimal number of balls of radius $2^{-n}$ covering $[T]$ is the number of distinct length-$n$ prefixes, which is at most $|T_n|$ and equals it when every accepted prefix extends. Then
$\log N(2^{-n})/\log(2^{n})=\log_2|T_n|/n=\delta_T(n)$,
and the upper box dimension of $[T]$ is $\limsup_n\delta_T(n)=\dimT T$. For the periodic density theories below the prefix-closure hypothesis holds exactly, so $\dimT$ is genuinely the box dimension of a compact subset of Cantor space.
\end{remark}

\section{Universal bounds}\label{sec:bounds}

\begin{lemma}[Logarithmic bound]\label{lem:logbound}
For every theory $T$ and every $n$, $\log_2\count(T,n)\le n$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $\count(T,n)=0$ the left side is $0\le n$ by Convention~\ref{conv:log0}. Otherwise $1\le\count(T,n)\le 2^n$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:trivial} and monotonicity of $\log_2$ on the positives gives $\log_2\count(T,n)\le\log_2 2^n=n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Estimates lie in the unit interval]\label{lem:estunit}
For every theory $T$: $\delta_T(n)\ge 0$ for all $n$, and $\delta_T(n)\le 1$ for all $n\ge 1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Nonnegativity: the denominator is nonnegative; the numerator is $0$ when the count is $0$, and otherwise $\log_2$ of an integer $\ge 1$, hence $\ge 0$. Upper bound: divide Lemma~\ref{lem:logbound} by $n>0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Universal bounds]\label{prop:bounds}
For every theory $T$, $\ 0\le\dimT T\le 1$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:estunit} the family $(\delta_T(n))_n$ is eventually bounded above by $1$, so the $\limsup$ is a well-defined real number at most $1$; it is bounded below pointwise by $0$, so the $\limsup$ is at least $0$. (Boundedness above makes the $\limsup$ finite; coboundedness below legitimises the $\limsup$ manipulations used later.)
\end{proof}

Both bounds are attained (Corollary~\ref{cor:landmark}), so Proposition~\ref{prop:bounds} cannot be improved.

\section{Monotonicity}\label{sec:mono}

\begin{lemma}[Counts are monotone]\label{lem:countmono}
If $T_n\subseteq T'_n$ for all $n$, then $\count(T,n)\le\count(T',n)$ for all $n$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Cardinality is monotone under inclusion of finite sets.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Estimates are monotone]\label{lem:estmono}
Under the same hypothesis, $\delta_T(n)\le\delta_{T'}(n)$ for all $n$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Denominators agree and are nonnegative, so compare numerators. If $\count(T,n)=0$ the left numerator is $0$ by Convention~\ref{conv:log0} while the right numerator is $\ge 0$. Otherwise both counts are positive and monotonicity of $\log_2$ transfers Lemma~\ref{lem:countmono}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity of dimension]\label{thm:mono}
If $T_n\subseteq T'_n$ for all $n$, then $\dimT T\le\dimT T'$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$\delta_T\le\delta_{T'}$ pointwise by Lemma~\ref{lem:estmono}, and both families satisfy the boundedness and coboundedness conditions established in Proposition~\ref{prop:bounds}, so the $\limsup$ comparison applies.
\end{proof}

Thus $\dimT$ is an order-preserving map from the inclusion order on theories to $[0,1]$. It is not injective and not a lattice homomorphism, but it is a genuine numerical invariant of the growth of a theory.

\section{Periodic density theories: exact combinatorics}\label{sec:comb}

\begin{definition}[Periodic density theory]
Let $m\ge 1$ and $R\subseteq\{0,\dots,m-1\}$. The \emph{periodic density theory} $D(m,R)$ has levels
\[
D(m,R)_n=\bigl\{\,x\in\{0,1\}^n \;:\; \forall i<n,\; (i\bmod m\notin R)\Rightarrow x_i=0\,\bigr\}.
\]
Coordinate $i$ is \emph{free} if $i\bmod m\in R$ and \emph{frozen} otherwise. Equivalently $D(m,R)_n=\prod_{i<n}A_i$ with $A_i=\{0,1\}$ for free $i$ and $A_i=\{0\}$ for frozen $i$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Free-coordinate count]
$F_{m,R}(n):=\#\{\,i\in\{0,\dots,n-1\} : i\bmod m\in R\,\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Exact counting law]\label{thm:count}
For all $m,R,n$: $\ \count(D(m,R),n)=2^{F_{m,R}(n)}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$D(m,R)_n$ is a Cartesian product of one- or two-element sets indexed by $i<n$: two elements at free coordinates, one at frozen ones. The cardinality of a product is the product of cardinalities, so
$\prod_{i<n}|A_i|=\prod_{i<n}2^{[i\text{ free}]}=2^{\sum_{i<n}[i\text{ free}]}=2^{F_{m,R}(n)}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Estimate is a free-coordinate ratio]\label{cor:ratio}
For $n\ge 1$: $\ \delta_{D(m,R)}(n)=F_{m,R}(n)/n$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Substitute Theorem~\ref{thm:count} and use $\log_2 2^k=k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Base case and monotonicity]\label{lem:Fmono}
$F_{m,R}(0)=0$, and $F_{m,R}$ is nondecreasing in $n$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The empty index range has no admissible index. Enlarging $n$ enlarges $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, hence the admissible subset, hence its cardinality.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Period relation]\label{thm:period}
If $R\subseteq\{0,\dots,m-1\}$ then $F_{m,R}(n+m)=F_{m,R}(n)+|R|$ for all $n$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Split $\{0,\dots,n+m-1\}=\{0,\dots,n-1\}\sqcup\{n,\dots,n+m-1\}$. The first block contributes $F_{m,R}(n)$. The second consists of $m$ consecutive integers, so $i\mapsto i\bmod m$ restricted to it is a bijection onto $\{0,\dots,m-1\}$: exactly $|R|$ of those indices are admissible, one for each residue in $R$ (here $R\subseteq\{0,\dots,m-1\}$ ensures every element of $R$ actually occurs as a residue).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exact value at multiples of the period]\label{cor:mult}
If $R\subseteq\{0,\dots,m-1\}$ then $F_{m,R}(mq)=|R|\,q$ for all $q\ge 0$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Induction on $q$: the case $q=0$ is $F_{m,R}(0)=0$, and
$F_{m,R}(m(q+1))=F_{m,R}(mq+m)=F_{m,R}(mq)+|R|=|R|q+|R|$
by Theorem~\ref{thm:period}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Two-sided sandwich]\label{thm:sandwich}
Let $m\ge 1$ and $R\subseteq\{0,\dots,m-1\}$. Then for all $n$,
\[
|R|\left\lfloor \frac{n}{m}\right\rfloor \;\le\; F_{m,R}(n) \;\le\; |R|\left\lfloor \frac{n}{m}\right\rfloor+|R|.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Put $q=\lfloor n/m\rfloor$. Lower bound: $mq\le n$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:Fmono} and Corollary~\ref{cor:mult} give $|R|q=F_{m,R}(mq)\le F_{m,R}(n)$. Upper bound: $n=mq+r$ with $0\le r<m$, hence $n\le m(q+1)$ and $F_{m,R}(n)\le F_{m,R}(m(q+1))=|R|q+|R|$.
\end{proof}

The gap between the bounds is the constant $|R|\le m$, independent of $n$.

\section{The Density Theorem}\label{sec:density}

\begin{theorem}[Quantitative convergence]\label{thm:quant}
Let $m\ge 1$ and $R\subseteq\{0,\dots,m-1\}$. Then for every $n\ge 1$,
\[
\left|\,\delta_{D(m,R)}(n)-\frac{|R|}{m}\,\right| \;\le\; \frac{|R|}{n}.
\]
Consequently $\delta_{D(m,R)}(n)\to|R|/m$ at rate $O(1/n)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write $F=F_{m,R}(n)$, $k=|R|$, $q=\lfloor n/m\rfloor$, and $n=mq+r$ with $0\le r<m$; by Corollary~\ref{cor:ratio} the estimate is $F/n$.

\emph{Upper deviation.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:sandwich}, $F\le kq+k$, and $mq\le n$ gives $q\le n/m$, so
$F/n\le (kn/m+k)/n=k/m+k/n$.

\emph{Lower deviation.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:sandwich}, $F\ge kq$, and $n=mq+r$ with $r<m$ gives $q\ge n/m-1$, so
$F/n\ge k(n/m-1)/n=k/m-k/n$.

Combining, $|F/n-k/m|\le k/n$; since $k$ is constant the bound tends to $0$, and any $n>k/\varepsilon$ makes the deviation smaller than $\varepsilon$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Density Theorem]\label{thm:density}
Let $m\ge 1$ and $R\subseteq\{0,\dots,m-1\}$. Then $\ \dimT D(m,R)=\dfrac{|R|}{m}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The finite-scale estimates converge to $|R|/m$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:quant}, and for a convergent sequence the $\limsup$ equals the limit.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Robustness]
No step used the \emph{identity} of the admissible residues, only their number $|R|$. The theories $D(3,\{0,1\})$ and $D(3,\{0,2\})$ are different sets of strings --- level $3$ of the first is $\{000,100,010,110\}$ and of the second $\{000,100,001,101\}$ --- and their counts differ at lengths that are not multiples of the period (at $n=2$ the first has $4$ elements and the second $2$); but by Corollary~\ref{cor:mult} they agree exactly at every multiple of $3$, and the sandwich confines the intermediate values to within the constant $|R|$, so both have dimension $2/3$. Dimension is blind to \emph{which} coordinates carry information and sensitive only to \emph{how many}; this is precisely what makes the realisation theorem possible.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Certified error bars]
Theorem~\ref{thm:quant} turns numerical experiments into proofs: computing $\delta_{D(m,R)}(n)$ at a single $n$ certifies the dimension to within $|R|/n$, with no hidden constant and no asymptotic caveat.
\end{remark}

\section{The dimension spectrum of truth}\label{sec:spectrum}

\begin{theorem}[Realisation Theorem]\label{thm:realise}
For all natural numbers $p\le q$ with $q\ge 1$ there is a theory $T$ with $\dimT T=p/q$; explicitly, $T=D(q,\{0,1,\dots,p-1\})$ works.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $R=\{0,\dots,p-1\}$. Since $p\le q$ we have $R\subseteq\{0,\dots,q-1\}$ and $|R|=p$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:density} with $m=q$ gives $\dimT D(q,R)=p/q$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Rational spectrum]\label{cor:spectrum}
Every rational number in $[0,1]$ is the fractal dimension of an explicitly constructible theory. The dimension spectrum $\mathcal{S}=\{\dimT T: T\text{ a theory}\}\subseteq[0,1]$ satisfies $[0,1]\cap\mathbb{Q}\subseteq\mathcal{S}$; in particular $\mathcal{S}$ is dense in $[0,1]$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Write a rational in $[0,1]$ as $p/q$ with $0\le p\le q$, $q\ge 1$, and apply Theorem~\ref{thm:realise}; density follows since $\mathcal S\subseteq[0,1]$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:bounds}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Landmark values; sharpness]\label{cor:landmark}
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\dimT D(1,\{0\})=1$: with modulus $1$ and the unique residue admissible every coordinate is free, each level is all of $\{0,1\}^n$, and the dimension is $1$.
\item $\dimT D(2,\{0\})=1/2$: the half-information theory, with even coordinates free and odd coordinates forced to $0$, has dimension exactly one half.
\item $\dimT D(1,\varnothing)=0$: with no admissible residue every coordinate is frozen, each level is the singleton $\{0^n\}$, and the dimension is $0$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular the bounds of Proposition~\ref{prop:bounds} are attained, so no strictly sharper universal bound exists.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Each is Theorem~\ref{thm:density} with the indicated $(m,R)$: $1/1$, $1/2$, $0/1$.
\end{proof}

The value $1/2$ that motivated this study is therefore not distinguished: it is the point of the spectrum at $(m,|R|)=(2,1)$, no more canonical than $3/7$ at $(7,3)$.

\begin{example}
$D(3,\{0,1\})$ --- free coordinates at positions $\equiv 0,1\pmod 3$ --- has dimension $2/3$; its counts for $n=0,1,2,\dots$ are $1,2,4,4,8,16,16,32,64,64,\dots$, i.e.\ $2^{F}$ with $F=0,1,2,2,3,4,4,5,6,6,\dots$.
\end{example}

\begin{example}
$D(7,\{0,1,2\})$ has dimension $3/7\approx 0.428571$. At $n=100$ we have $100=7\cdot 14+2$, so $F=3\cdot 14+\#\{r\in\{0,1,2\}:r<2\}=44$ and the estimate is $0.44$. Theorem~\ref{thm:quant} certifies $|0.44-3/7|\le 0.03$; the true error is $0.0114285\ldots$
\end{example}

\section{Algorithms}\label{sec:algorithms}

\subsection{Free-coordinate count}
The definition gives a direct $O(n)$ algorithm; the period structure gives one independent of $n$:
\[
F_{m,R}(n)=|R|\cdot\left\lfloor\frac{n}{m}\right\rfloor+\#\{\,r\in R : r< n\bmod m\,\}.
\]
Indeed, writing $n=mq+s$ with $s=n\bmod m$, the first $mq$ indices contribute $|R|q$ by Corollary~\ref{cor:mult}, and the remaining indices $mq,\dots,mq+s-1$ have residues $0,\dots,s-1$, so exactly the $r\in R$ with $r<s$ are counted. This closed form refines Theorem~\ref{thm:sandwich}: the correction term lies in $[0,|R|]$, recovering both bounds. Complexity: $O(|R|)$ arithmetic operations, or $O(1)$ after $O(m)$ preprocessing of a prefix-count table.

\subsection{Count and dimension estimate}
Given $F_{m,R}(n)$, the count is the exact integer $2^{F_{m,R}(n)}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:count}) and the finite-scale estimate is the exact rational $F_{m,R}(n)/n$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:ratio}). No floating-point logarithm is ever needed: the logarithm has been eliminated analytically.

\subsection{Certified dimension approximation}
To approximate $\dimT D(m,R)$ within $\varepsilon>0$, choose $n>|R|/\varepsilon$ and return $F_{m,R}(n)/n$; Theorem~\ref{thm:quant} guarantees the answer is within $\varepsilon$.

\subsection{Realising a target rational}
To construct a theory of dimension $p/q$, output $D(q,\{0,\dots,p-1\})$, i.e.\ the acceptance predicate ``$x_i=0$ whenever $i\bmod q\ge p$''. Membership testing on a length-$n$ string is $O(n)$; enumerating level $n$ is $O(2^{F_{m,R}(n)}\cdot n)$, optimal in the output size.

\section{Interpretation}\label{sec:interp}

\subsection{Dimension as compressibility}
Theorem~\ref{thm:count} puts $D(m,R)_n$ in explicit bijection with $\{0,1\}^{F_{m,R}(n)}$: read off the free coordinates and discard the frozen ones. A member of nominal length $n$ therefore carries only $F_{m,R}(n)\approx dn$ bits of content, $d=\dimT$. Three equivalent readings of the same number: \emph{counting} (about $2^{dn}$ statements of length $n$); \emph{density} (a fraction $d$ of coordinates are information-bearing); \emph{compression} (membership is a lossless compression scheme with ratio $d$). Dimension $1$ means incompressible; dimension $0$ means fully determined by the constraints.

\subsection{The role of the limsup}
For a general theory the finite estimates need not converge. Take coordinates free on blocks $[n_k,n_{k+1})$ for even $k$ and frozen for odd $k$, with $n_{k+1}/n_k\to\infty$: then $\delta_T(n)$ approaches $1$ along the ends of free blocks and $0$ along the ends of frozen blocks, and no limit exists. The $\limsup$ still lies in $[0,1]$ and records the most generous asymptotic rate. A parallel lower box dimension via $\liminf$ records the least generous rate; the two agree for asymptotically regular theories, and Theorem~\ref{thm:quant} shows the periodic density theories are regular.

\subsection{The empty-level convention}
The choice $\log_2 0=0$ is not cosmetic. Without it $\delta_T(n)$ is undefined at empty levels and Theorem~\ref{thm:mono} cannot even be stated for theories with gaps. With it, an empty level contributes the minimal estimate $0$: a level with no statements adds no exponential content and can only push the dimension down. It also makes $\dimT$ insensitive to the difference between ``one statement per length'' and ``no statements at some lengths'' --- the expected coarseness of an exponential-rate invariant.

\subsection{Comparison with the classical Cantor set}
The middle-thirds Cantor set has box dimension $\log 2/\log 3\approx 0.6309$, an irrational number obtained from a self-similar scaling construction. The periodic density theories are also Cantor-type subsets of $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ --- closed, perfect when $R\ne\varnothing$, nowhere dense when $R\ne\{0,\dots,m-1\}$ --- but their construction is \emph{coordinatewise} rather than by scaling: each coordinate is free or frozen, an all-or-nothing decision. That binary decision is why the achievable dimensions of the periodic family are exactly the rationals with denominator dividing the period; irrationality returns only when periodicity is broken.

\section{Extensions and future work}\label{sec:future}

\subsection{Arbitrary densities and irrational dimensions}
Let $S\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ be any set of free coordinates and $D(S)$ the theory accepting strings vanishing off $S$. Exactly as in Theorem~\ref{thm:count}, $|D(S)_n|=2^{|S\cap[0,n)|}$, so $\delta_{D(S)}(n)$ is the finite-window density of $S$ and
$\dimT D(S)=\overline{\mathrm d}(S)$, the upper asymptotic density of $S$. Since every real $d\in[0,1]$ is the density of some set of naturals --- e.g.\ the Beatty-type set $S=\{i:\lfloor (i+1)d\rfloor>\lfloor id\rfloor\}$ --- the full dimension spectrum is all of $[0,1]$. Periodicity buys the explicit $O(1/n)$ error bound of Theorem~\ref{thm:quant}, which for general $S$ has no uniform analogue.

\subsection{Beyond product theories}
All theories analysed here are \emph{products}: acceptance is a conjunction of independent per-coordinate constraints. The general problem is to compute $\dimT T$ for correlated constraints --- for instance strings accepted by a fixed finite automaton, where $|T_n|$ grows like $\lambda^n$ for $\lambda$ the Perron root of the transition matrix, giving $\dimT T=\log_2\lambda$, generally irrational. This suggests a hierarchy: product theories give rationals, regular theories give logarithms of algebraic numbers, and richer classes give more.

\subsection{Deductively closed theories}
The framework imposes no closure. Deductive closure creates correlations between coordinates (a proved statement forces its consequences to be present), so the product theories are not deductively closed and the realisation theorem does not transfer directly. Determining the dimension spectrum of deductively closed theories is open.

\subsection{Dimension as a complexity-theoretic invariant}
If $T$ is the set of yes-instances of a decision problem in binary, $\dimT T$ measures the density of yes-instances on the exponential scale: sparse languages have dimension $0$. Making precise the behaviour of $\dimT$ under length-preserving polynomial-time reductions, and asking whether it separates natural classes, connects this combinatorics to resource-bounded dimension theory.

\subsection{Multifractal refinement}
Rather than a single exponent, one may weight statements (by proof length, logical depth, or a probability measure on the theory) and study the multifractal spectrum $f(\alpha)$ of local dimensions; for periodic density theories with a nonuniform measure a Legendre-transform computation should give an explicit spectrum.

\section{Conclusion}

We have equipped the space of theories with a numerical size invariant --- the box-counting dimension of the associated subset of Cantor space --- and determined its behaviour completely on an explicit family. The invariant lies in $[0,1]$, is monotone under inclusion, and attains both endpoints. For a periodic density theory with modulus $m$ and admissible residue set $R$ the dimension is exactly the density $|R|/m$ of information-bearing coordinates, proved via the exact counting law $|D(m,R)_n|=2^{F_{m,R}(n)}$, the period relation $F_{m,R}(n+m)=F_{m,R}(n)+|R|$, and a sandwich that squeezes the finite estimates to the density with error at most $|R|/n$. Consequently every rational in $[0,1]$ is realised as a dimension by an explicit construction: the dimension spectrum of truth contains the whole rational unit interval, and the isolated value $1/2$ found earlier is one point among a dense set of company.

The proofs are elementary but the framework is not: it converts a vague question --- how big is a body of mathematics? --- into an exact combinatorial one, with a computable answer, certified error bars at every finite scale, and a clear roadmap for the correlated cases where the answer is not yet known.

  "demo": """"
The Dimension Spectrum of Truth — numerical demonstrations.

Statements of length n are bit strings in {0,1}^n.  A *theory* assigns to each
length n a set of accepted strings T_n.  Its fractal (box-counting) dimension is

    dim T = limsup_n  log2 |T_n| / n.

For the *periodic density theory* D(m, R) — coordinate i is free iff i mod m is
in R, and frozen (forced to 0) otherwise — the development proves:

    (1) exact counting law        |D(m,R)_n| = 2 ** F(n),   F(n) = #{i<n : i%m in R}
    (2) period relation           F(n+m) = F(n) + |R|
    (3) two-sided sandwich        |R|*floor(n/m) <= F(n) <= |R|*floor(n/m) + |R|
    (4) quantitative convergence  | F(n)/n - |R|/m |  <=  |R| / n
    (5) Density Theorem           dim D(m,R) = |R| / m
    (6) Realization Theorem       every rational p/q in [0,1] is a dimension,
                                  realized by D(q, {0,...,p-1})
    (7) monotonicity              T subset T'  =>  dim T <= dim T'
    (8) universal bounds          0 <= dim T <= 1, both attained

This script verifies all of them numerically, by brute-force enumeration at
small lengths and by the closed forms at large ones.

Run:  python3 demo.py          (pure standard library, no dependencies)
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import product
from math import log2, floor, gcd
from typing import Dict, Iterator, List, Set, Tuple


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core definitions
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def is_free(i: int, m: int, R: Set[int]) -> bool:
    """Coordinate i is information-bearing iff its residue mod m is admissible."""
    return (i % m) in R


def enumerate_level(n: int, m: int, R: Set[int]) -> Iterator[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Brute-force enumeration of level n of the periodic density theory D(m,R)."""
    choices: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = [
        (0, 1) if is_free(i, m, R) else (0,) for i in range(n)
    ]
    yield from product(*choices)


def count_bruteforce(n: int, m: int, R: Set[int]) -> int:
    """|D(m,R)_n| computed by enumerating every accepted string."""
    return sum(1 for _ in enumerate_level(n, m, R))


def free_count_naive(n: int, m: int, R: Set[int]) -> int:
    """F(n) = #{ i < n : i mod m in R }, computed directly.  O(n)."""
    return sum(1 for i in range(n) if is_free(i, m, R))


def free_count_closed(n: int, m: int, R: Set[int]) -> int:
    """F(n) via the closed form  |R|*floor(n/m) + #{r in R : r < n mod m}.  O(|R|)."""
    q, s = divmod(n, m)
    return len(R) * q + sum(1 for r in R if r < s)


def count_exact(n: int, m: int, R: Set[int]) -> int:
    """|D(m,R)_n| = 2 ** F(n), the exact counting law (no enumeration)."""
    return 2 ** free_count_closed(n, m, R)


def dim_estimate(n: int, m: int, R: Set[int]) -> Fraction:
    """Finite-scale estimate log2(count)/n, which equals the exact rational F(n)/n."""
    if n == 0:
        return Fraction(0)
    return Fraction(free_count_closed(n, m, R), n)


def dim_estimate_via_log(n: int, m: int, R: Set[int]) -> float:
    """The same estimate computed the 'naive' way, through a floating-point log."""
    if n == 0:
        return 0.0
    c = count_exact(n, m, R)
    return (0.0 if c == 0 else log2(c)) / n


def box_dimension(m: int, R: Set[int]) -> Fraction:
    """dim D(m,R) = |R| / m  (Density Theorem)."""
    return Fraction(len(R), m)


def sandwich_bounds(n: int, m: int, R: Set[int]) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """The proved two-sided bounds  |R|*floor(n/m) <= F(n) <= |R|*floor(n/m) + |R|."""
    lo = len(R) * (n // m)
    return lo, lo + len(R)


def certified_length(m: int, R: Set[int], eps: Fraction) -> int:
    """Smallest n guaranteeing |estimate(n) - dim| <= eps, from the O(1/n) bound."""
    if len(R) == 0:
        return 1
    return max(1, floor(Fraction(len(R)) / eps) + 1)


def realize_rational(p: int, q: int) -> Tuple[int, Set[int]]:
    """Realization Theorem: D(q, {0,...,p-1}) has dimension exactly p/q."""
    assert 0 <= p <= q and q >= 1
    return q, set(range(p))

def demo_counting_law() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("1. EXACT COUNTING LAW:  |D(m,R)_n| = 2^F(n)")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("   Brute-force enumeration vs. the closed formula.\n")
    for (m, R) in [(2, {0}), (3, {0, 1}), (4, {1, 3}), (5, {0})]:
        print(f"   m = {m}, R = {sorted(R)}   (predicted dimension {len(R)}/{m})")
        header = "     n : " + "".join(f"{n:>7d}" for n in range(9))
        print(header)
        brute = [count_bruteforce(n, m, R) for n in range(9)]

        print("  F(n) : " + "".join(f"{f:>7d}" for f in free))
        print(" brute : " + "".join(f"{c:>7d}" for c in brute))
        print(" 2^F(n): " + "".join(f"{c:>7d}" for c in exact))
        assert brute == exact, "counting law failed"
        print("     -> agreement at every length. OK\n")


def demo_period_and_sandwich() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("2. PERIOD RELATION  F(n+m) = F(n) + |R|   AND THE TWO-SIDED SANDWICH")
    print("=" * 74)
    m, R = 7, {0, 2, 5}
    print(f"   m = {m}, R = {sorted(R)}, |R| = {len(R)}\n")
    print("      n   F(n)  F(n+m)  F(n)+|R|   lower <= F(n) <= upper")
    for n in range(0, 30, 3):
        f = free_count_closed(n, m, R)
        f_shift = free_count_closed(n + m, m, R)
        lo, hi = sandwich_bounds(n, m, R)
        assert f_shift == f + len(R), "period relation failed"
        assert lo <= f <= hi, "sandwich failed"
        print(f"   {n:4d}  {f:5d}  {f_shift:6d}  {f + len(R):8d}      {lo:3d} <= {f:3d} <= {hi:3d}")
    print("\n   -> period relation and sandwich hold at every tested n. OK\n")


def demo_convergence() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("3. QUANTITATIVE CONVERGENCE:  |F(n)/n - |R|/m|  <=  |R|/n")
    print("=" * 74)
    m, R = 7, {0, 1, 2}
    d = box_dimension(m, R)
    print(f"   Theory D({m}, {sorted(R)}),  dimension = {d} = {float(d):.9f}\n")
    print("        n     estimate F(n)/n      float log2 route     |error|      bound |R|/n")
    for n in [1, 2, 5, 10, 100, 1_000, 10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000]:
        est = dim_estimate(n, m, R)
        err = abs(est - d)
        bound = Fraction(len(R), n)
        via_log = dim_estimate_via_log(n, m, R) if n <= 10_000 else float("nan")
        assert err <= bound, "convergence bound violated"
        log_str = f"{via_log:>18.12f}" if n <= 10_000 else " " * 12 + "(skipped)"
        print(f"   {n:8d}   {float(est):>16.12f} {log_str}   {float(err):.3e}   {float(bound):.3e}")
    print("\n   -> the certified error bar |R|/n always dominates the true error. OK\n")

    print("=" * 74)
    print("4. REALIZATION THEOREM: every rational in [0,1] is a dimension")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("   For each target p/q we build D(q, {0,...,p-1}) and measure it.\n")
    print("     target      m   R                     dim      estimate n=20000    error")
    targets = [(0, 1), (1, 5), (1, 3), (3, 7), (1, 2), (5, 8), (2, 3), (9, 10), (1, 1)]

        if not R:
            rs = "{}"
        print(f"     {p:>2d}/{q:<3d}   {m:>3d}   {rs:<20s} {str(d):>6s}   {float(est):>16.10f}   {float(abs(est - d)):.2e}")
    print("\n   -> every rational target is realized exactly. OK\n")

def demo_monotonicity() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("6. MONOTONICITY:  T subset T'  =>  dim T <= dim T'")
    print("=" * 74)
    m = 12

    print("      R                                   dim     level-24 count   nested?")
    prev_level: Set[Tuple[int, ...]] | None = None
    prev_dim = Fraction(-1)
    for k in range(0, m + 1, 2):

def demo_identity_blindness() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("7. DIMENSION SEES ONLY HOW MANY COORDINATES ARE FREE, NOT WHICH")
    print("=" * 74)
    m = 5
    from itertools import combinations
    print("   Counts at intermediate lengths DO depend on which residues are free,")
    print("   but they coincide at every multiple of the period, and so do the dimensions.\n")
    for k in range(m + 1):
        sets = [set(R) for R in combinations(range(m), k)]
        # counts at multiples of the period are identical across all choices of R
        counts_at_periods = {tuple(count_exact(m * q, m, R) for q in range(5)) for R in sets}
        dims = {box_dimension(m, R) for R in sets}

        assert max(spread) - min(spread) <= k, "sandwich gap exceeded"
        print(f"   |R| = {k}: all C({m},{k}) = {len(sets):>2d} residue sets share dimension "

              f" and F(7) spread {min(spread)}..{max(spread)} (<= |R| = {k})")
    print("\n   -> only the cardinality |R| matters asymptotically; this is why every")

def demo_compression_reading() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("8. DIMENSION AS A COMPRESSION RATIO")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("   An accepted string of length n is determined by its F(n) free bits,")
    print("   so membership in the theory is a lossless code of ratio ~ dim.\n")
    m, R = 8, {0, 3, 6}
    n = 64
    F = free_count_closed(n, m, R)
    d = box_dimension(m, R)
    sample = tuple(1 if is_free(i, m, R) and i % 3 == 0 else 0 for i in range(n))
    packed = tuple(sample[i] for i in range(n) if is_free(i, m, R))
    restored = [0] * n
    j = 0
    for i in range(n):
        if is_free(i, m, R):
            restored[i] = packed[j]
            j += 1
    assert tuple(restored) == sample, "round-trip failed"
    print(f"   theory D({m}, {sorted(R)}),  dimension {d} = {float(d):.4f}")

from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import product
from math import log2, floor, gcd
from typing import Dict, Iterator, List, Set, Tuple


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core definitions
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def is_free(i: int, m: int, R: Set[int]) -> bool:
    """Coordinate i is information-bearing iff its residue mod m is admissible."""
    return (i % m) in R


def enumerate_level(n: int, m: int, R: Set[int]) -> Iterator[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Brute-force enumeration of level n of the periodic density theory D(m,R)."""
    choices: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = [
        (0, 1) if is_free(i, m, R) else (0,) for i in range(n)
    ]
    yield from product(*choices)


def count_bruteforce(n: int, m: int, R: Set[int]) -> int:
    """|D(m,R)_n| computed by enumerating every accepted string."""
    return sum(1 for _ in enumerate_level(n, m, R))


def free_count_naive(n: int, m: int, R: Set[int]) -> int:
    """F(n) = #{ i < n : i mod m in R }, computed directly.  O(n)."""
    return sum(1 for i in range(n) if is_free(i, m, R))


def free_count_closed(n: int, m: int, R: Set[int]) -> int:
    """F(n) via the closed form  |R|*floor(n/m) + #{r in R : r < n mod m}.  O(|R|)."""
    q, s = divmod(n, m)
    return len(R) * q + sum(1 for r in R if r < s)


def count_exact(n: int, m: int, R: Set[int]) -> int:
    """|D(m,R)_n| = 2 ** F(n), the exact counting law (no enumeration)."""
    return 2 ** free_count_closed(n, m, R)


def dim_estimate(n: int, m: int, R: Set[int]) -> Fraction:
    """Finite-scale estimate log2(count)/n, which equals the exact rational F(n)/n."""
    if n == 0:
        return Fraction(0)
    return Fraction(free_count_closed(n, m, R), n)


def dim_estimate_via_log(n: int, m: int, R: Set[int]) -> float:
    """The same estimate computed the 'naive' way, through a floating-point log."""
    if n == 0:
        return 0.0
    c = count_exact(n, m, R)
    return (0.0 if c == 0 else log2(c)) / n


def box_dimension(m: int, R: Set[int]) -> Fraction:
    """dim D(m,R) = |R| / m  (Density Theorem)."""
    return Fraction(len(R), m)


def sandwich_bounds(n: int, m: int, R: Set[int]) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """The proved two-sided bounds  |R|*floor(n/m) <= F(n) <= |R|*floor(n/m) + |R|."""
    lo = len(R) * (n // m)
    return lo, lo + len(R)


def certified_length(m: int, R: Set[int], eps: Fraction) -> int:
    """Smallest n guaranteeing |estimate(n) - dim| <= eps, from the O(1/n) bound."""
    if len(R) == 0:
        return 1
    return max(1, floor(Fraction(len(R)) / eps) + 1)

    """Realization Theorem: D(q, {0,...,p-1}) has dimension exactly p/q."""
    assert 0 <= p <= q and q >= 1
    return q, set(range(p))

    """All reduced p/q in [0,1] with 1 <= q <= Q, in increasing order."""
    fs = {(p, q) for q in range(1, Q + 1) for p in range(0, q + 1) if gcd(p, q) == 1}

*A guided tour of the fractal dimension of truth — from counting bit strings to a complete
description of every dimension a theory can have.*

---

## 1. The wrong question, and the right one

Ask how many true statements there are and you get a useless answer: infinitely many, and
the same infinity for every interesting theory. Ask instead **how fast** the true statements
accumulate as you allow longer and longer descriptions, and something measurable appears.

Fix an encoding that writes every statement as a finite string of bits — exactly what a
computer does before it can store a mathematical claim. Among the $2^n$ possible strings of
length $n$, a given body of mathematics accepts some sub-collection. Write $\mathrm{count}(T,n)$
for how many it accepts. If that number behaves like $2^{dn}$, then the single number $d$ is
what we are after.

$$
\dim T \;=\; \limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{\log_2 \mathrm{count}(T,n)}{n}.
$$

<details>
<summary><b>Why this is literally a fractal dimension</b> (click to expand)</summary>

Think of an infinite bit sequence as a point in [Cantor space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_space)
$\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$, with the distance between two sequences defined as $2^{-i}$ where $i$ is the
first coordinate at which they differ. In that metric, a ball of radius $2^{-n}$ is exactly a
*cylinder*: the set of all sequences sharing a fixed prefix of length $n$. So the number of balls
of radius $2^{-n}$ needed to cover our theory is precisely $\mathrm{count}(T,n)$.

The [box-counting dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minkowski%E2%80%93Bouligand_dimension) of a set is
$$\lim_{\varepsilon \to 0}\frac{\log N(\varepsilon)}{\log(1/\varepsilon)},$$
and substituting $\varepsilon = 2^{-n}$ turns it into $\log_2 \mathrm{count}(T,n)/n$. The "growth rate of
truth" and "the fractal dimension of truth" are the same number, not an analogy.
</details>

Two facts pin down the scale immediately.

- **Every theory has dimension between $0$ and $1$.** A theory cannot accept more than all
  $2^n$ strings, so $\log_2 \mathrm{count}(T,n) \le n$ and every finite estimate is at most $1$;
  counts are never negative, so every estimate is at least $0$.
- **Bigger theories have bigger dimension.** If one theory accepts everything another
  accepts, its counts are at least as large at every length, so its dimension is at least as
  large. Dimension respects inclusion.

---

## 2. Play with it first

Before any proofs: here is the whole subject in one panel. Pick a period $m$, click residue
classes to make coordinates **free** (either bit allowed) or **frozen** (forced to $0$), and
watch the dimension move. Try the presets, then try to hit $5/9$ by hand.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

1. The dimension readout is always the plain fraction $|R|/m$ — the number of green chips

2. The number of accepted statements is always an exact power of two, $2^{F(n)}$, where $F(n)$

## 3. The construction, precisely

**Definition.** Fix a modulus $m \ge 1$ and a set of admissible residues $R \subseteq \{0,\dots,m-1\}$.
The *periodic density theory* $D(m,R)$ accepts a length-$n$ string $x$ exactly when
$$
x_i = 0 \quad\text{for every } i < n \text{ with } i \bmod m \notin R .
$$
Coordinate $i$ is **free** if $i \bmod m \in R$ and **frozen** otherwise.

Let $F(n) = \#\{ i < n : i \bmod m \in R\}$ be the number of free coordinates below $n$.

**The exact counting law.** $\mathrm{count}(D(m,R),n) = 2^{F(n)}$.

*Why:* acceptance is a conjunction of independent single-coordinate constraints, so the
accepted set is a Cartesian product with two options at each free coordinate and one at each
frozen one. The cardinality of a product is the product of the cardinalities.

This one line does most of the work: it eliminates the logarithm entirely, so the
finite-scale estimate is the exact rational $F(n)/n$ and no floating-point arithmetic ever
enters.

---

## 4. From an exact count to a dimension

Three short steps take us from the counting law to the answer.

<details>
<summary><b>Step 1 — Periodicity: sliding the window adds exactly $|R|$ free coordinates</b></summary>

$$F(n+m) = F(n) + |R|.$$

Split the index range $\{0,\dots,n+m-1\}$ into $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ and the block
$\{n,\dots,n+m-1\}$. The block consists of $m$ consecutive integers, so reducing them mod $m$
gives each residue $0,\dots,m-1$ exactly once — a *complete residue system*. Exactly $|R|$ of
them are admissible.
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Step 2 — Exactness at multiples of the period, then a sandwich</b></summary>

Iterating Step 1 from $F(0)=0$ gives $F(mq) = |R|\,q$ exactly. Since $F$ is nondecreasing and
every $n$ lies between $m\lfloor n/m\rfloor$ and $m(\lfloor n/m\rfloor+1)$,
$$
|R| \left\lfloor \frac{n}{m} \right\rfloor \;\le\; F(n) \;\le\; |R| \left\lfloor \frac{n}{m} \right\rfloor + |R| .
$$
The two ends differ by the constant $|R|$, no matter how large $n$ is.
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Step 3 — The squeeze, with an explicit error bar</b></summary>

Divide the sandwich by $n$ and use $m\lfloor n/m\rfloor \le n \le m(\lfloor n/m\rfloor+1)$:
$$
\left| \frac{F(n)}{n} - \frac{|R|}{m} \right| \;\le\; \frac{|R|}{n} \qquad \text{for every } n \ge 1 .
$$
The right-hand side tends to $0$, so the estimates *converge* — the upper limit is an honest
limit here — and the convergence rate is $O(1/n)$ with no hidden constant.
</details>

> ### The Density Theorem
> For every modulus $m \ge 1$ and every set of admissible residues $R \subseteq \{0,\dots,m-1\}$,
> $$\dim D(m,R) = \frac{|R|}{m},$$
> the asymptotic density of information-bearing coordinates.

Here is that theorem as a picture: six theories converging to six different asymptotes, and
one of them shown inside its certified corridor.

{{visualization:0}}

---

## 5. The punchline: every rational is a dimension

Notice what the argument never used: *which* residues are admissible. Only *how many*. So we
can dial the ratio to anything we like.

> ### The Realization Theorem
> For natural numbers $p \le q$ with $q \ge 1$, the theory of modulus $q$ that frees exactly the
> residues $\{0,1,\dots,p-1\}$ has dimension exactly $p/q$. Hence **every rational number in
> $[0,1]$ is the fractal dimension of an explicitly constructed theory.**

This is a recipe, not an existence proof. Want dimension $3/7$? Free the coordinates congruent
to $0,1,2$ modulo $7$ and freeze the rest.

{{visualization:1}}

The three landmark values are now instances of one law rather than separate curiosities:

| construction | dimension | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| modulus $1$, every residue free | $1$ | the full space; statements are incompressible |
| modulus $2$, one residue free | $1/2$ | the half-information theory |
| modulus $1$, no residue free | $0$ | one statement per length; nothing is left to choose |

Both endpoints are attained, so the universal bounds $0 \le \dim T \le 1$ are sharp. And the
value $1/2$, which motivated the whole investigation, turns out to be no more canonical than
$3/7$.

---

## 6. What the number *means*: compression

The counting law puts the accepted strings of length $n$ in explicit bijection with
$\{0,1\}^{F(n)}$ — read off the free coordinates and throw away the frozen ones. So a statement
of nominal length $n$ carries only about $dn$ bits of real content, where $d$ is the dimension.

Three readings of one number:

- **counting** — about $2^{dn}$ statements of length $n$;
- **density** — a fraction $d$ of coordinates are information-bearing;
- **compression** — membership in the theory is a [lossless code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lossless_compression)
  of ratio $d$.

Dimension $1$ means incompressible: knowing a string is accepted tells you nothing. Dimension
$0$ means the theory's constraints already determine everything.

The suite below verifies all of this numerically — including a pack/unpack round trip that
exhibits the compression explicitly — and checks every inequality proved above against brute-force
enumeration.

{{demo:0}}

---

## 7. Computing it: exactly, and fast

Naively, measuring a theory's dimension means enumerating $2^n$ strings per length. For periodic
density theories we can do infinitely better, because the closed form
$$
F(n) \;=\; |R| \left\lfloor \frac{n}{m} \right\rfloor \;+\; \#\{\, r \in R : r < n \bmod m \,\}
$$
computes everything in $O(|R|)$ arithmetic operations, independent of $n$ — and it refines the
sandwich, since the correction term lies in $[0,|R|]$.

{{algorithm:0}}

Reverse the question and you get the design problem: *given* a target dimension, build the
theory. The construction is uniform, with no search and no approximation.

{{algorithm:1}}

For contrast, here is the honest baseline for an arbitrary theory presented only as a
membership oracle — exponential in the horizon, which is exactly why structure pays.

{{algorithm:2}}

---

## 8. Why an *upper* limit?

A pedantic-looking detail in the definition earns its keep. For a general theory the finite
estimates need not converge at all.

<details>
<summary><b>An oscillating theory, in detail</b></summary>

Free a coordinate $i$ exactly when $\lfloor \log_2 (i+1) \rfloor$ is even. The free and frozen blocks
then double in length at every stage, so the density of free coordinates below $n$ is high at
the end of a free block and low at the end of a frozen one — permanently, with no damping. The
exact counting law still holds (acceptance is still a per-coordinate constraint); what fails is
convergence.

Make the blocks grow faster than geometrically and the estimates approach $1$ along one
subsequence and $0$ along another. There is no limit. The $\limsup$ still exists in $[0,1]$ and
records the theory's most generous asymptotic rate — which is why the definition uses it.
</details>

Run the comparison yourself: an oscillating theory next to a periodic one converging inside its
error bar.

{{demo:1}}

<details>
<summary><b>One more convention: what if a level is empty?</b></summary>

If a theory accepts nothing at some length, its count is $0$ and $\log_2 0$ is undefined. The
convention here is $\log_2 0 = 0$, so an empty level contributes the smallest possible estimate.
That is exactly right for monotonicity: an empty level can only push the dimension down, never
up. It also means the invariant cannot distinguish "one statement per length" from "no statements
at some lengths" — both give $0$ — which is the expected coarseness of an exponential-rate
measure.
</details>

---

## 9. Where this goes next

The theories analysed here are all **products**: acceptance is a conjunction of independent
per-coordinate constraints, which is precisely what makes the count a pure power of two. Relax
that and the picture changes:

- **Aperiodic patterns.** Free an arbitrary set $S$ of coordinates and the same argument gives
  dimension equal to the upper asymptotic density of $S$; since every real in $[0,1]$ is such a
  density, the full spectrum is the whole interval. What periodicity buys is the explicit
  $O(1/n)$ error bar.
- **Correlated constraints.** For strings accepted by a fixed finite automaton the count grows
  like $\lambda^n$ with $\lambda$ the [Perron root](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perron%E2%80%93Frobenius_theorem)
  of the transition matrix, giving dimension $\log_2 \lambda$ — generally irrational.
- **Deductive closure.** Closure creates correlations between coordinates, so the product
  constructions are not closed. Which dimensions survive is open.
- **Complexity.** For a language of yes-instances, the dimension measures the density of
  yes-instances on the exponential scale; sparse languages have dimension $0$.
- **Multifractality.** Weighting statements non-uniformly should produce a whole spectrum
  $f(\alpha)$ of local dimensions, with the single number here as its maximum.

---

## 10. Take-away

A body of mathematics has a size, and it is a number in $[0,1]$: the exponential rate at which
its statements accumulate, equivalently the density of the bits it leaves free, equivalently the
factor by which its statements compress. The number is monotone under enlarging the theory, it
attains both endpoints, and — the content of the main theorem — every rational value is realized
by a construction you can write down in one line and check by hand.

The next time someone asks how big a theory is, hand them a number.

# Average Discrepancy of Codes for Hamming Balls

This file formalizes the *rigorous combinatorial kernel* behind the conjecture on the
discrepancy of random linear codes for all Hamming balls.

## Background (the conjecture)

For a finite field `𝔽_q`, integers `n`, `ρ ∈ (0,1)` and `ε > 0`, one takes a random
linear code `C ⊆ 𝔽_q^n` of dimension `k = ⌈(1 - (1/n)·log_q |B_ρ| + ε)·n⌉` and asks
that, with probability `1-o(1)`, simultaneously for *every* centre `z`,
`|C ∩ B_ρ(z)| = (1 ± o(1)) · |C| · |B_ρ| / q^n`.

The target value `|C| · |B_ρ| / q^n` is exactly the count one would expect if `C` were
a uniformly random set of its size, and the ball `B_ρ(z)` had volume `|B_ρ|` independent
of its centre.

## What is proved here (the unconditional kernel)

The heart of the "first moment" of that statement is a *deterministic, exact* identity:
for **any** subset `C` of the group `G = ι → α` (no linearity, no randomness), the
average over all centres `z` of `|C ∩ B_r(z)|` equals exactly `|C| · |B_r| / |G|`.

* `hammingDist_add_right` — Hamming distance is translation invariant.
* `ball_card_eq` — the ball volume `|B_r(z)|` is independent of the centre `z`.
* `sum_inter_ball` — **exact averaging identity**: `∑_z |C ∩ B_r(z)| = |C| · |B_r|`.
* `card_bad_centres_le` — a one-sided (Markov) discrepancy bound: the centres where
  `|C ∩ B_r(z)|` is at least `t` number at most `|C| · |B_r| / t`.

These isolate precisely the part of the conjecture that holds with certainty; the
remaining gap (per-centre concentration) is what genuinely needs randomness/linearity.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): The claimed target value `|C|·|B_ρ|/q^n` is not merely a
heuristic; it is the *exact average* of `|C ∩ B_ρ(z)|` over all centres, for every set
`C`.  If true, the conjecture is exactly a concentration-around-the-mean statement.

Experiment (Experimenter): Formalize the double counting
`∑_z |C ∩ B_r(z)| = ∑_{c∈C} #{z : d(c,z) ≤ r} = ∑_{c∈C} |B_r(c)| = |C|·|B_r|`,
using translation invariance to get `|B_r(c)| = |B_r(0)|`.

Analysis (Analyst): The averaging identity is unconditional and dimension-free; it
needs *no* algebraic structure beyond a group acting by translation.  This shows the
"hard" content of the conjecture is purely the upper/lower tail concentration over the
`q^n` centres, not the value of the mean.  The Markov bound `card_bad_centres_le`
already gives one half (the upper tail for all-but-few centres) for free.

Critique (Critic): The identity is exact, not vacuous: it computes a genuine double sum
and is false if the ball volume depended on the centre, which is why translation
invariance is isolated as a load-bearing lemma.  Linearity of `C` is deliberately *not*
assumed, making the statement strictly more general than the conjecture's hypothesis.
-/

namespace HammingBallDiscrepancy

open Finset

variable {ι : Type*} {α : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι] [DecidableEq α] [Fintype α]

section Group
variable [AddGroup α]

omit [DecidableEq ι] [Fintype α] in
/-- Hamming distance is invariant under right translation by a common vector `a`. -/
theorem hammingDist_add_right (x y a : ι → α) :
    hammingDist (x + a) (y + a) = hammingDist x y := by
  unfold hammingDist
  congr 1
  ext i
  simp [add_left_inj]

/-- The Hamming ball of radius `r` about centre `z` inside `G = ι → α`. -/
def ball (r : ℕ) (z : ι → α) : Finset (ι → α) :=
  Finset.univ.filter (fun x => hammingDist x z ≤ r)

omit [AddGroup α] in
@[simp]
theorem mem_ball {r : ℕ} {z x : ι → α} :
    x ∈ ball r z ↔ hammingDist x z ≤ r := by
  simp [ball]

/-- The ball about `z` is the translate by `z` of the ball about `0`. -/
theorem ball_eq_image (r : ℕ) (z : ι → α) :
    ball r z = (ball r 0).image (· + z) := by
  ext x
  simp only [mem_ball, mem_image]
  constructor
  · intro hx
    refine ⟨x - z, ?_, sub_add_cancel x z⟩
    have h := hammingDist_add_right (x - z) 0 z
    simp only [sub_add_cancel, zero_add] at h
    rw [← h]; exact hx
  · rintro ⟨y, hy, rfl⟩
    have h := hammingDist_add_right y 0 z
    simp only [zero_add] at h
    rw [h]; exact hy

/-- **Ball volume is independent of the centre.** -/
theorem ball_card_eq (r : ℕ) (z : ι → α) :
    (ball r z).card = (ball r (0 : ι → α)).card := by
  rw [ball_eq_image]
  exact Finset.card_image_of_injective _ (add_left_injective z)

/-- The number of centres `z` whose ball of radius `r` contains a fixed point `c`
equals the ball volume. -/
theorem card_centres_containing (r : ℕ) (c : ι → α) :
    (Finset.univ.filter (fun z => hammingDist c z ≤ r)).card
      = (ball r (0 : ι → α)).card := by
  have hset : (Finset.univ.filter (fun z => hammingDist c z ≤ r)) = ball r c := by
    ext z
    simp only [ball, mem_filter, Finset.mem_univ, true_and]
    rw [hammingDist_comm]
  rw [hset, ball_card_eq]

/-- **Exact averaging identity.** For any subset `C`, the total count of pairs
`(c, z)` with `c ∈ C` and `c` in the ball of radius `r` about `z` equals
`|C| · |B_r|`; equivalently the average over centres `z` of `|C ∩ B_r(z)|` is
exactly `|C| · |B_r| / |G|`. -/
theorem sum_inter_ball (C : Finset (ι → α)) (r : ℕ) :
    ∑ z, (C ∩ ball r z).card = C.card * (ball r (0 : ι → α)).card := by
  have hcount : ∀ z, (C ∩ ball r z).card
      = ∑ c ∈ C, (if hammingDist c z ≤ r then 1 else 0) := by
    intro z
    have heq : C ∩ ball r z = C.filter (fun c => hammingDist c z ≤ r) := by
      ext c
      simp [ball, Finset.mem_inter]
    rw [heq, Finset.card_filter]
  simp_rw [hcount]
  rw [Finset.sum_comm]
  have hinner : ∀ c ∈ C, (∑ z, (if hammingDist c z ≤ r then 1 else 0))
      = (ball r (0 : ι → α)).card := by
    intro c _
    rw [← Finset.card_filter]
    exact card_centres_containing r c
  rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl hinner, Finset.sum_const, smul_eq_mul, mul_comm]

/-- **One-sided (Markov) discrepancy bound.** For any threshold `t`, the centres `z`

theorem card_bad_centres_le (C : Finset (ι → α)) (r t : ℕ) :
    (Finset.univ.filter (fun z => t ≤ (C ∩ ball r z).card)).card * t
      ≤ C.card * (ball r (0 : ι → α)).card := by

        rw [Finset.sum_const, smul_eq_mul]

        apply Finset.sum_le_sum
        intro z hz
        exact (Finset.mem_filter.mp hz).2
    _ ≤ ∑ z, (C ∩ ball r z).card := by
        apply Finset.sum_le_sum_of_subset
        exact Finset.filter_subset _ _

end Group

# Adaptive Fluctuation-Robust Demon Impossibility

`Catalog/Computation/FluctuationRobustDemon.lean` proved a Chernoff-type large-deviation
bound

```
P( ∑_{i<n} W_i ≤ n·w )  ≤  exp ( -n·β·(ΔF - w) )
```

(`FluctDemon.product_jarzynski`), so it says nothing about a demon that *adapts*: one that
inspects the outcome of the first erasure before choosing how to perform the second.
Adaptivity is exactly what a computational control strategy has, so closing this gap is
what turns the bound into a statement about algorithms.

This file removes the independence hypothesis, which was Conjecture 2 of the previous
cycle's `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md`.  An adaptive demon is modelled by a finite decision tree
(`FluctDemon.AdaptiveDemon`): at each of `n` stages it runs a finite work system whose
choice may depend on the entire history of observed outcomes.  The main theorem
`FluctDemon.adaptive_deficit_bound` shows that the *same* exponential bound holds — indeed
in the sharper, threshold-free form

```
P( total work ≤ t )  ≤  exp ( -β·(n·ΔF - t) ),

for the supermartingale `exp(-β ∑_{i≤k} W_i + kβΔF)`.

## Main definitions

* `FluctDemon.AdaptiveDemon` — an `n`-stage history-dependent control strategy.
* `FluctDemon.AdaptiveDemon.Compliant` — every node obeys the Jarzynski equality at `(β, ΔF)`.
* `FluctDemon.AdaptiveDemon.deficitProb` — the probability that the total work over all `n`
  stages is at most `t`.
* `FluctDemon.AdaptiveDemon.meanTotalWork` — the expected total work.
* `FluctDemon.AdaptiveDemon.expWorkAvg` — the tree-level Jarzynski average
  `⟨e^{-β·(total work)}⟩`.

## Main results

* `FluctDemon.AdaptiveDemon.expWorkAvg_eq` — **adaptive tensorisation**: a compliant
  `n`-stage strategy satisfies the Jarzynski equality at cost `n·ΔF` *exactly*, adaptivity
  notwithstanding.
* `FluctDemon.adaptive_deficit_bound_of_dissipative`, `FluctDemon.adaptive_deficit_bound` —
  **main theorem**: `P(total work ≤ t) ≤ exp(-β(n·ΔF - t))` for every adaptive strategy each
  of whose stages dissipates at least `ΔF` (in particular for every Jarzynski-compliant one).
* `FluctDemon.adaptive_deficit_concentration` — the `t = n·w` form, matching (and
  strictly generalising) `FluctDemon.deficit_concentration`.
* `FluctDemon.adaptive_meanWork_ge` — expectation-level second law for adaptive strategies.
* `FluctDemon.adaptive_reliability_bound`, `FluctDemon.adaptive_deficit_tendsto_zero` — an
  adaptive demon succeeding with probability `≥ δ` can only handle `n ≤ log(1/δ)/(β(ΔF-w))`
  bits, and its success probability tends to `0`.
* `FluctDemon.coinStage_deficitProb`, `FluctDemon.trueAdaptiveCoin_deficitProb` — an
  explicitly *history-dependent* witness: its one-stage sub-threshold probability is exactly
  `1/2` and its two-stage one exactly `1/4`, against the bound `(2/3)² = 4/9`.  So the
  theorem is not vacuous and the bound is not attained trivially.
-/

open Finset Real

noncomputable section

namespace FluctDemon

variable {Ω : Type*} [Fintype Ω]

/-! ## Adaptive strategies as finite decision trees -/

/-- An **adaptive demon** with `n` remaining stages: at each stage it runs a finite work
system, observes the outcome, and chooses the strategy for the remaining stages as a
function of that outcome.  Unfolding the recursion, the protocol used at stage `k` depends
on the whole history `ω₁,…,ω_{k-1}`, so this is the fully general finite-memory adaptive
control strategy. -/
inductive AdaptiveDemon (Ω : Type*) [Fintype Ω] : ℕ → Type _
  /-- The empty strategy: no stages left. -/
  | done : AdaptiveDemon Ω 0
  /-- Run `S`, then continue with `next ω` after observing outcome `ω`. -/
  | step {n : ℕ} (S : WorkSystem Ω) (next : Ω → AdaptiveDemon Ω n) : AdaptiveDemon Ω (n + 1)

namespace AdaptiveDemon

/-- Every stage of the strategy — for every history — obeys the Jarzynski equality at
inverse temperature `β` and free-energy cost `ΔF`. -/
def Compliant (β ΔF : ℝ) : ∀ {n : ℕ}, AdaptiveDemon Ω n → Prop
  | _, .done => True
  | _, .step S next => Jarzynski β ΔF S ∧ ∀ ω, Compliant β ΔF (next ω)

/-- A weaker, one-sided compliance: every stage merely **dissipates at least** `ΔF`, in the
sense of the Jarzynski *inequality* `⟨e^{-βW}⟩ ≤ e^{-βΔF}`.  Genuine Jarzynski compliance is
the special case of equality. -/
def Dissipative (β ΔF : ℝ) : ∀ {n : ℕ}, AdaptiveDemon Ω n → Prop
  | _, .done => True
  | _, .step S next => expAvg β S ≤ Real.exp (-β * ΔF) ∧ ∀ ω, Dissipative β ΔF (next ω)

/-- Jarzynski compliance implies the one-sided dissipativity condition. -/
theorem Compliant.dissipative {β ΔF : ℝ} :
    ∀ {n : ℕ} {D : AdaptiveDemon Ω n}, D.Compliant β ΔF → D.Dissipative β ΔF := by
  intro n
  induction n with
  | zero => intro D _; cases D; exact trivial
  | succ n ih =>
      intro D hD
      cases D with
      | step S next =>
          obtain ⟨hS, hnext⟩ := hD
          exact ⟨le_of_eq hS, fun ω => ih (hnext ω)⟩

/-- The probability that the **total** work accumulated over all remaining stages is at
most `t`.  Computed by conditioning on the first outcome: the threshold for the remaining
stages is lowered by the work just spent. -/
def deficitProb : ∀ {n : ℕ}, AdaptiveDemon Ω n → ℝ → ℝ
  | _, .done, t => if 0 ≤ t then 1 else 0
  | _, .step S next, t => ∑ ω, S.prob ω * deficitProb (next ω) (t - S.work ω)

/-- The Jarzynski exponential average `⟨e^{-β·(total work)}⟩` of an adaptive strategy. -/
def expWorkAvg (β : ℝ) : ∀ {n : ℕ}, AdaptiveDemon Ω n → ℝ
  | _, .done => 1
  | _, .step S next =>
      ∑ ω, S.prob ω * (Real.exp (-β * S.work ω) * expWorkAvg β (next ω))

/-- The expected total work of an adaptive strategy. -/
def meanTotalWork : ∀ {n : ℕ}, AdaptiveDemon Ω n → ℝ
  | _, .done => 0
  | _, .step S next => ∑ ω, S.prob ω * (S.work ω + meanTotalWork (next ω))

@[simp] lemma deficitProb_done (t : ℝ) :
    (AdaptiveDemon.done (Ω := Ω)).deficitProb t = if 0 ≤ t then 1 else 0 := rfl

@[simp] lemma deficitProb_step {n : ℕ} (S : WorkSystem Ω) (next : Ω → AdaptiveDemon Ω n)
    (t : ℝ) :
    (AdaptiveDemon.step S next).deficitProb t
      = ∑ ω, S.prob ω * (next ω).deficitProb (t - S.work ω) := rfl

@[simp] lemma expWorkAvg_done (β : ℝ) : expWorkAvg β (AdaptiveDemon.done (Ω := Ω)) = 1 := rfl

@[simp] lemma expWorkAvg_step (β : ℝ) {n : ℕ} (S : WorkSystem Ω)
    (next : Ω → AdaptiveDemon Ω n) :
    expWorkAvg β (AdaptiveDemon.step S next)
      = ∑ ω, S.prob ω * (Real.exp (-β * S.work ω) * expWorkAvg β (next ω)) := rfl

@[simp] lemma meanTotalWork_done : meanTotalWork (AdaptiveDemon.done (Ω := Ω)) = 0 := rfl

@[simp] lemma meanTotalWork_step {n : ℕ} (S : WorkSystem Ω) (next : Ω → AdaptiveDemon Ω n) :
    meanTotalWork (AdaptiveDemon.step S next)
      = ∑ ω, S.prob ω * (S.work ω + meanTotalWork (next ω)) := rfl

/-- Deficit probabilities are genuine probabilities: nonnegative. -/
theorem deficitProb_nonneg : ∀ {n : ℕ} (D : AdaptiveDemon Ω n) (t : ℝ), 0 ≤ D.deficitProb t := by
  intro n
  induction n with
  | zero =>
      intro D t
      cases D
      simp only [deficitProb_done]
      split <;> norm_num
  | succ n ih =>
      intro D t
      cases D with
      | step S next =>
          simp only [deficitProb_step]
          exact Finset.sum_nonneg fun ω _ => mul_nonneg (S.prob_nonneg ω) (ih (next ω) _)

/-- Deficit probabilities are genuine probabilities: at most `1`. -/
theorem deficitProb_le_one : ∀ {n : ℕ} (D : AdaptiveDemon Ω n) (t : ℝ), D.deficitProb t ≤ 1 := by
  intro n
  induction n with
  | zero =>
      intro D t
      cases D
      simp only [deficitProb_done]
      split <;> norm_num
  | succ n ih =>
      intro D t
      cases D with
      | step S next =>
          simp only [deficitProb_step]
          calc ∑ ω, S.prob ω * (next ω).deficitProb (t - S.work ω)
              ≤ ∑ ω, S.prob ω * 1 :=
                Finset.sum_le_sum fun ω _ =>
                  mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left (ih (next ω) _) (S.prob_nonneg ω)
            _ = 1 := by simpa using S.prob_sum

/-- **Adaptive tensorisation of the Jarzynski equality.**  If every node of an `n`-stage
adaptive strategy obeys the Jarzynski equality at cost `ΔF`, then the total work of the
whole strategy obeys it at cost `n · ΔF` — *exactly*, and with no independence assumption
whatsoever.  This is the finite decision-tree form of the statement that
`exp(-β ∑_{i ≤ k} W_i + kβΔF)` is a martingale. -/
theorem expWorkAvg_eq {β ΔF : ℝ} :
    ∀ {n : ℕ} (D : AdaptiveDemon Ω n), D.Compliant β ΔF →
      expWorkAvg β D = Real.exp (-β * ((n : ℝ) * ΔF)) := by
  intro n
  induction n with
  | zero =>
      intro D _
      cases D
      simp
  | succ n ih =>
      intro D hD
      cases D with
      | step S next =>
          obtain ⟨hS, hnext⟩ := hD
          simp only [expWorkAvg_step]
          have hsub : ∀ ω : Ω, expWorkAvg β (next ω) = Real.exp (-β * ((n : ℝ) * ΔF)) :=
            fun ω => ih (next ω) (hnext ω)
          calc ∑ ω, S.prob ω * (Real.exp (-β * S.work ω) * expWorkAvg β (next ω))
              = Real.exp (-β * ((n : ℝ) * ΔF)) *
                  ∑ ω, S.prob ω * Real.exp (-β * S.work ω) := by
                rw [Finset.mul_sum]
                exact Finset.sum_congr rfl fun ω _ => by rw [hsub ω]; ring
            _ = Real.exp (-β * ((n : ℝ) * ΔF)) * Real.exp (-β * ΔF) := by
                rw [show ∑ ω, S.prob ω * Real.exp (-β * S.work ω) = expAvg β S from rfl, hS]
            _ = Real.exp (-β * (((n : ℝ) + 1) * ΔF)) := by
                rw [← Real.exp_add]; congr 1; ring
            _ = Real.exp (-β * (((n + 1 : ℕ) : ℝ) * ΔF)) := by push_cast; ring_nf

end AdaptiveDemon

/-! ## The adaptive concentration theorem -/

/-- **Fluctuation-robust demon impossibility, adaptive version.**

For *every* adaptive finite-memory control strategy whose every stage obeys a
Jarzynski/Crooks-type fluctuation relation at free-energy cost `ΔF`, the probability that
the total work over `n` stages falls below `t` is at most `exp(-β·(n·ΔF - t))`.

No independence is assumed: the protocol used at each stage may depend arbitrarily on all
previously observed outcomes.  The bound involves only `β, ΔF, t, n`, so it is uniform
over all strategies, in particular over all polynomial-time ones.

This version assumes only the one-sided condition `Dissipative` (`⟨e^{-βW}⟩ ≤ e^{-βΔF}` at
every stage); `adaptive_deficit_bound` is the Jarzynski-equality corollary. -/
theorem adaptive_deficit_bound_of_dissipative {β ΔF : ℝ} (hβ : 0 < β) :
    ∀ {n : ℕ} (D : AdaptiveDemon Ω n), D.Dissipative β ΔF → ∀ t : ℝ,
      D.deficitProb t ≤ Real.exp (-β * ((n : ℝ) * ΔF - t)) := by
  intro n
  induction n with
  | zero =>
      intro D _ t
      cases D
      simp only [AdaptiveDemon.deficitProb_done, Nat.cast_zero, zero_mul, zero_sub]
      by_cases h : 0 ≤ t
      · rw [if_pos h]
        have h1 : (1 : ℝ) = Real.exp 0 := by simp
        rw [h1]
        exact Real.exp_le_exp.mpr (by nlinarith)
      · rw [if_neg h]
        exact le_of_lt (Real.exp_pos _)
  | succ n ih =>
      intro D hD t
      cases D with
      | step S next =>
          obtain ⟨hS, hnext⟩ := hD
          simp only [AdaptiveDemon.deficitProb_step]
          have hterm : ∀ ω : Ω,
              S.prob ω * (next ω).deficitProb (t - S.work ω)
                ≤ S.prob ω *
                  (Real.exp (-β * ((n : ℝ) * ΔF - t)) * Real.exp (-β * S.work ω)) := by
            intro ω
            refine mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left ?_ (S.prob_nonneg ω)
            refine le_trans (ih (next ω) (hnext ω) (t - S.work ω)) (le_of_eq ?_)
            rw [← Real.exp_add]; congr 1; ring
          calc ∑ ω, S.prob ω * (next ω).deficitProb (t - S.work ω)
              ≤ ∑ ω, S.prob ω *
                  (Real.exp (-β * ((n : ℝ) * ΔF - t)) * Real.exp (-β * S.work ω)) :=
                Finset.sum_le_sum fun ω _ => hterm ω
            _ = Real.exp (-β * ((n : ℝ) * ΔF - t)) *
                  ∑ ω, S.prob ω * Real.exp (-β * S.work ω) := by
                rw [Finset.mul_sum]
                exact Finset.sum_congr rfl fun ω _ => by ring
            _ ≤ Real.exp (-β * ((n : ℝ) * ΔF - t)) * Real.exp (-β * ΔF) := by
                rw [show ∑ ω, S.prob ω * Real.exp (-β * S.work ω) = expAvg β S from rfl]
                exact mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left hS (le_of_lt (Real.exp_pos _))
            _ = Real.exp (-β * (((n + 1 : ℕ) : ℝ) * ΔF - t)) := by
                rw [← Real.exp_add]; push_cast; congr 1; ring

/-- **Fluctuation-robust demon impossibility, adaptive version.**  The Jarzynski-compliant
special case of `adaptive_deficit_bound_of_dissipative`. -/
theorem adaptive_deficit_bound {β ΔF : ℝ} (hβ : 0 < β) {n : ℕ} (D : AdaptiveDemon Ω n)
    (hD : D.Compliant β ΔF) (t : ℝ) :
    D.deficitProb t ≤ Real.exp (-β * ((n : ℝ) * ΔF - t)) :=
  adaptive_deficit_bound_of_dissipative hβ D hD.dissipative t

/-- **Adaptive concentration at a per-bit threshold.**  Taking `t = n · w`, an adaptive
demon spends less than `w` per erased bit with probability at most `exp(-n β (ΔF - w))`:
exactly the bound of `FluctDemon.deficit_concentration`, now without independence. -/
theorem adaptive_deficit_concentration {β ΔF w : ℝ} (hβ : 0 < β) {n : ℕ}
    (D : AdaptiveDemon Ω n) (hD : D.Compliant β ΔF) :
    D.deficitProb ((n : ℝ) * w) ≤ Real.exp (-(n : ℝ) * β * (ΔF - w)) := by
  refine le_trans (adaptive_deficit_bound hβ D hD ((n : ℝ) * w)) (le_of_eq ?_)
  congr 1
  ring

/-- **Expectation-level second law for adaptive strategies.**  A compliant `n`-stage
adaptive demon spends at least `n · ΔF` work on average. -/
theorem adaptive_meanWork_ge {β ΔF : ℝ} (hβ : 0 < β) :
    ∀ {n : ℕ} (D : AdaptiveDemon Ω n), D.Compliant β ΔF →
      (n : ℝ) * ΔF ≤ D.meanTotalWork := by
  intro n
  induction n with
  | zero =>
      intro D _
      cases D
      simp
  | succ n ih =>
      intro D hD
      cases D with
      | step S next =>
          obtain ⟨hS, hnext⟩ := hD
          simp only [AdaptiveDemon.meanTotalWork_step]
          have hsplit : ∑ ω, S.prob ω * (S.work ω + (next ω).meanTotalWork)
              = meanWork S + ∑ ω, S.prob ω * (next ω).meanTotalWork := by
            rw [show meanWork S = ∑ ω, S.prob ω * S.work ω from rfl, ← Finset.sum_add_distrib]
            exact Finset.sum_congr rfl fun ω _ => by ring
          have htail : (n : ℝ) * ΔF ≤ ∑ ω, S.prob ω * (next ω).meanTotalWork := by
            have hle : ∀ ω : Ω, S.prob ω * ((n : ℝ) * ΔF)
                ≤ S.prob ω * (next ω).meanTotalWork := fun ω =>
              mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left (ih (next ω) (hnext ω)) (S.prob_nonneg ω)
            have hconst : ∑ ω, S.prob ω * ((n : ℝ) * ΔF) = (n : ℝ) * ΔF := by
              rw [← Finset.sum_mul, S.prob_sum, one_mul]
            calc (n : ℝ) * ΔF = ∑ ω, S.prob ω * ((n : ℝ) * ΔF) := hconst.symm
              _ ≤ ∑ ω, S.prob ω * (next ω).meanTotalWork :=
                  Finset.sum_le_sum fun ω _ => hle ω
          have hhead : ΔF ≤ meanWork S := meanWork_ge_of_jarzynski hβ hS
          rw [hsplit]
          push_cast
          linarith

/-- **Reliability bound for an adaptive demon.**  If an adaptive strategy erases `n` bits
with total work below `n · w` (with `w < ΔF`) and succeeds with probability at least
`δ > 0`, then `n ≤ log(1/δ) / (β (ΔF - w))`.  Adaptivity buys the demon nothing. -/
theorem adaptive_reliability_bound {β ΔF w δ : ℝ} (hβ : 0 < β) (hw : w < ΔF) (hδ : 0 < δ)
    {n : ℕ} (D : AdaptiveDemon Ω n) (hD : D.Compliant β ΔF)
    (hsucc : δ ≤ D.deficitProb ((n : ℝ) * w)) :
    (n : ℝ) ≤ Real.log (1 / δ) / (β * (ΔF - w)) := by
  have hr : 0 < β * (ΔF - w) := by nlinarith
  have hδle : δ ≤ Real.exp (-(n : ℝ) * β * (ΔF - w)) :=
    le_trans hsucc (adaptive_deficit_concentration hβ D hD)
  have hlog : Real.log δ ≤ -(n : ℝ) * β * (ΔF - w) := by
    have := Real.log_le_log hδ hδle
    rwa [Real.log_exp] at this
  rw [le_div_iff₀ hr]
  have hinv : Real.log (1 / δ) = -Real.log δ := by rw [one_div, Real.log_inv]
  rw [hinv]
  nlinarith

/-- **The adaptive demon fails in the long run.**  For any target accuracy `ε > 0` there is
an `N` beyond which *every* adaptive strategy on `n ≥ N` bits has sub-threshold probability
below `ε`. -/
theorem adaptive_deficit_tendsto_zero {β ΔF w : ℝ} (hβ : 0 < β) (hw : w < ΔF) {ε : ℝ}
    (hε : 0 < ε) :
    ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ (n : ℕ), N ≤ n → ∀ (Ω : Type) [Fintype Ω] (D : AdaptiveDemon Ω n),
      D.Compliant β ΔF → D.deficitProb ((n : ℝ) * w) < ε := by
  have hr : 0 < β * (ΔF - w) := by nlinarith
  obtain ⟨N, hN⟩ := exists_nat_gt (Real.log (1 / ε) / (β * (ΔF - w)))
  refine ⟨N + 1, ?_⟩
  intro n hn Ω _ D hD
  refine lt_of_le_of_lt (adaptive_deficit_concentration hβ D hD) ?_
  have hnN : Real.log (1 / ε) / (β * (ΔF - w)) < (n : ℝ) := by
    have : (N : ℝ) < (n : ℝ) := by
      exact_mod_cast Nat.lt_of_lt_of_le (Nat.lt_succ_self N) hn
    linarith
  have hkey : Real.log (1 / ε) < (n : ℝ) * (β * (ΔF - w)) := (div_lt_iff₀ hr).mp hnN
  have hlt : Real.exp (-(n : ℝ) * β * (ΔF - w)) < Real.exp (-Real.log (1 / ε)) := by
    apply Real.exp_lt_exp.mpr
    nlinarith
  refine lt_of_lt_of_le hlt (le_of_eq ?_)
  rw [← Real.log_inv]
  simp [Real.exp_log hε]

/-! ## A genuinely history-dependent witness -/

section Witness

variable {β ΔF : ℝ}

/-- The one-stage strategy running the catalog's `coinDemon`. -/
def coinStage (β ΔF : ℝ) : AdaptiveDemon Bool 1 :=
  .step (coinDemon β ΔF) (fun _ => .done)

/-- A **genuinely adaptive** two-stage demon: after the cheap outcome it retries the coin
protocol, after the expensive one it runs a deterministic protocol that pays exactly the
free-energy cost.  The two stages therefore use *different* work systems depending on the
observed history, so this strategy is outside the scope of the independent-product theorem
`FluctDemon.deficit_concentration`. -/
def surePay (ΔF : ℝ) : WorkSystem Bool where
  prob := fun b => cond b 0 1
  work := fun _ => ΔF
  prob_nonneg := fun b => by cases b <;> norm_num
  prob_sum := by simp

/-- `surePay` obeys the Jarzynski equality: it always pays exactly `ΔF`. -/
theorem surePay_jarzynski : Jarzynski β ΔF (surePay ΔF) := by
  unfold Jarzynski expAvg surePay
  rw [Fintype.sum_bool]
  simp

/-- The genuinely adaptive two-stage demon. -/
def trueAdaptiveCoin (β ΔF : ℝ) : AdaptiveDemon Bool 2 :=
  .step (coinDemon β ΔF)
    (fun b => cond b (.step (surePay ΔF) (fun _ => .done))
                     (.step (coinDemon β ΔF) (fun _ => .done)))

theorem coinStage_compliant (hβ : 0 < β) : (coinStage β ΔF).Compliant β ΔF :=
  ⟨coinDemon_jarzynski hβ, fun _ => trivial⟩

theorem trueAdaptiveCoin_compliant (hβ : 0 < β) :
    (trueAdaptiveCoin β ΔF).Compliant β ΔF := by
  refine ⟨coinDemon_jarzynski hβ, ?_⟩
  intro b
  cases b
  · exact ⟨coinDemon_jarzynski hβ, fun _ => trivial⟩
  · exact ⟨surePay_jarzynski, fun _ => trivial⟩

/-- **Non-vacuity.**  On a single stage the coin demon really does appear to beat the
free-energy threshold, with probability exactly `1/2`. -/
theorem coinStage_deficitProb (hβ : 0 < β) :
    (coinStage β ΔF).deficitProb (ΔF - Real.log (3 / 2) / β) = 1 / 2 := by
  have hlog2 : 0 < Real.log 2 := Real.log_pos (by norm_num)
  have hlog32 : 0 < Real.log (3 / 2) := Real.log_pos (by norm_num)
  have h1 : 0 < Real.log 2 / β := div_pos hlog2 hβ
  have h2 : 0 < Real.log (3 / 2) / β := div_pos hlog32 hβ
  simp only [coinStage, AdaptiveDemon.deficitProb_step, AdaptiveDemon.deficitProb_done,
    Fintype.sum_bool, coinDemon]
  simp only [Bool.cond_true, Bool.cond_false]
  split_ifs
  all_goals first
    | (exfalso; linarith)
    | norm_num

/-- The exact two-stage sub-threshold probability of the genuinely adaptive demon is `1/4`:
after the expensive first outcome the strategy can no longer recover, and after the cheap
one it succeeds only if the coin is cheap again. -/
theorem trueAdaptiveCoin_deficitProb (hβ : 0 < β) :
    (trueAdaptiveCoin β ΔF).deficitProb ((2 : ℝ) * (ΔF - Real.log (3 / 2) / β)) = 1 / 4 := by
  have hlog2 : 0 < Real.log 2 := Real.log_pos (by norm_num)
  have hlog32 : 0 < Real.log (3 / 2) := Real.log_pos (by norm_num)
  have h1 : 0 < Real.log 2 / β := div_pos hlog2 hβ
  have h2 : 0 < Real.log (3 / 2) / β := div_pos hlog32 hβ
  simp only [trueAdaptiveCoin, AdaptiveDemon.deficitProb_step, AdaptiveDemon.deficitProb_done,
    Fintype.sum_bool, coinDemon, surePay, Bool.cond_true, Bool.cond_false]
  split_ifs
  all_goals first
    | (exfalso; linarith)
    | norm_num

/-- Yet the adaptive bound already squeezes the two-stage genuinely adaptive demon: its
probability of averaging below `ΔF - log(3/2)/β` per bit is at most `(2/3)²`. -/
theorem trueAdaptiveCoin_bound (hβ : 0 < β) :
    (trueAdaptiveCoin β ΔF).deficitProb ((2 : ℝ) * (ΔF - Real.log (3 / 2) / β))
      ≤ Real.exp (-(2 : ℝ) * Real.log (3 / 2)) := by
  have h := adaptive_deficit_concentration (β := β) (ΔF := ΔF)
      (w := ΔF - Real.log (3 / 2) / β) hβ (trueAdaptiveCoin β ΔF)
      (trueAdaptiveCoin_compliant hβ)
  have hcast : ((2 : ℕ) : ℝ) = (2 : ℝ) := by norm_num
  rw [hcast] at h
  refine le_trans h (le_of_eq ?_)
  congr 1
  field_simp
  ring

end Witness
